title: Florida State's defensive keys vs Alabama
description: Florida State needs a big performance from their defense against a capable Alabama offense. Here are their keys on that side of the ball.
fullText:
The Florida State Seminoles are in danger of starting the season 1-2 as they travel to face the No. 10 Alabama Crimson Tide this Saturday in Tuscaloosa. They're also on a nine-game losing streak on the road, which doesn't give a lot that of confidence that they can win this matchup.

For this upset to happen, FSU is going to need an inspired performance from its defensive unit. Through the first two games of the season, that side of the ball hasn't shown the consistency or growth that defenses under Tony White typically display in the second year under his watch.

Alabama's offense is capable of putting up a ton of points, and the game could get out of hand quickly if Florida State doesn't come to play. Here are five keys for the Seminoles' defense.

Russell has dual-threat capabilities, and letting him be effective in multiple areas will spell doom for FSU's defense. He will make plays, but the Seminoles can't afford to be on the field for long periods of time due to Russell moving the chains with his arm and his legs. They must keep him in the pocket as much as possible.

Hill is coming off his first 100-yard game against the Kentucky Wildcats. He has enough explosion to his game to be a very tough player to deal with, and if he's keeping the chains moving, Florida State will be vulnerable against the pass as things will open up. Stopping Hill should be a high priority for Tony White.

This has been an area of concern for FSU's defense this season so far. They've allowed a conversion rate of 58.1%, which is 135th in the FBS. Also, they have the worst EPA per play defensively in the nation at -1.33, and four of the five passing touchdowns they've surrendered have come on third down. They have to get off the field against Alabama.

This is an area that Florida State was expected to lean on in 2026. However, they haven't consistently gotten pressure on the quarterback, and SMU pushed them around for 155 yards rushing. In order for FSU to have a chance, guys like Daniel Lyons, Mandrell Desir, and Denante McCray must show up in a big way.

The Crimson Tide have been able to wear down their first two opponents by averaging over 35 minutes of possession time. It will be paramount for Florida State to end drives early, which speaks to being good on third down, which will keep Alabama in their own territory.

This was an area that FSU was supposed to lean on in 2026. However, the Seminoles haven't consistently gotten pressure on the quarterback, and against SMU, they were pushed around for 155 yards.

fullText:
For around 15 hours, immigration detention officers kept Raúl Suárez Herrero confined in a cage slightly larger than a phone booth, where he feared snakes and endured mosquitoes in the middle of Florida swampland, the former detainee alleged.

Suárez, 59, told José Díaz-Balart in an interview for Noticias Telemundo’s “Ahora 360” that he was forced into the cage, measuring 7 feet, 9 inches high and 4 feet, 3 inches square, for praying out loud for an ill young man at “Alligator Alcatraz,” an ICE detention site.

“I feel like I was in hell,” Suárez later told NBC News in a phone interview from Mexico, where he was deported.

Suárez spoke days after a Department of Homeland Security watchdog confirmed the use of the phone booth-sized cages at the now-shuttered Florida detention camp in a Sept. 11 report.

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report said.

The DHS Office of Inspector General report documented its inspectors’ findings during an unannounced January visit to the Ochopee, Florida, site.

In December, Amnesty International issued its own report on conditions at the detention site based on interviews with detainees and its own tour of the facility. The organization detailed the use of the small cages and said it amounted to torture.

The facility staff told inspectors that the cages were “calming areas” where immigrants could de-escalate and have time alone and that no one spent more than two hours inside them.

But Suárez told Noticias Telemundo that “they took me there and I spent more than 15 hours inside in that little hole,” referring to the small cage. He said he was forced in around 1 p.m. and taken out at about 5 a.m. “when morning was breaking.” According to Suárez, the cage was in a recreation area where detainees took exercise time. Suárez said he couldn’t stretch out on the cage floor and got little sleep for fear of what might slither into the cage.

“I had to be careful because on the ground there were snakes and you don’t see them. You can’t fall asleep because they can come into the cage,” Suárez said in a video interview.

DHS did not directly address Suárez’s allegations or case in response to questions from NBC News. But a spokesperson rejected “claims that there were ‘inhumane’ conditions” at the immigrant detention center. Those claims are “categorically false” and any allegations of excessive use of force are “FALSE,” the spokesperson said in an email.

“No detainees were being beaten or abused,” the DHS spokesperson said. DHS provides long-standing medical, dental and mental health services, three meals a day that are evaluated by certified dietitians, clean water, clothing, bedding and hygiene products and access to phones to talk with family and lawyers, the spokesperson stated.

Alligator Alcatraz’s standards were consistent with those under other administrations, the spokesperson also said. Further questions were referred to the state of Florida, “as this facility was managed by the State of Florida through the Division of Emergency Management.”

The facility in the heart of the Everglades was built by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis as part of the state’s push to support President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

Alex Lafranconi, a spokesman for DeSantis, has dismissed criticism of the small cages. Lafranconi has described the small cages as a confinement area for “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful,” and said “we’d make them smaller, if we could.”

Although DHS said the inspector general “indicated” all recommendations have been administratively closed, the OIG said in its report that the administration did not address its 10 recommendations, including that it “discontinue the use of the small metal enclosures to hold detainees for any reason or amount of time.”

The OIG also said that at the time of the inspection, all the detainees were ICE detainees and there was evidence that ICE had some degree of oversight authority and engagement at the facility.

Originally from Cuba and in the U.S. since he was 12, Suárez was detained by ICE in July 2025 during an ICE check-in.

Before it was recently ordered closed, Alligator Alcatraz had been denounced by multiple detainees and legal and immigrant advocates for its conditions.

The detention facility’s records state the average time people were placed in the smaller cages with metal fencing was 59 minutes and 27 seconds, according to the OIG report. But the OIG said it could not confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding use of the enclosures or detainees’ allegations they had been denied food or other abuses.

The small cages at the facility were supposed to be a “safe and secure place” where people could “reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress, and practice self-directed behavior,” according to the detention camp’s policies, the report stated.

According to detention center records cited by the OIG, 79 people were held in the small cages during the period of July 17, 2025, to Jan. 18, and none were held more than two hours. Detainees in the small cage “may leave at any time by detainee request or per staff directive,” according to the report.

But Suárez was adamant that his confinement was not voluntary and lasted far more than two hours.

“Everybody lied” about the small cages, Suárez said, disputing that he could have gotten out or requested to be let out.

He said he was forced into the cage after praying out loud for a man who had an epileptic seizure as they were waiting to get registered at the detention camp.

Help for the man was taking “too long,” according to Suárez. That’s when he said he started praying aloud, as he used to do at the evangelical church he attended before his arrest.

“I asked God for the young man’s life,” he said.

Suárez alleged two guards then forced him to stand up, asked where he was from and then grabbed him and dragged him “all the way back to where that little cell was.” He said he was kicked in the leg so hard he thought they broke it. “My leg was so big and black.”

“They just dropped me over there and locked the doors,” he said. He said he got no medical treatment for his leg or a medical evaluation after the confinement.

Suárez said his experience has left him psychologically “shattered.”

Suárez was removed to Mexico in February after more than four decades of living in the United States. He was detained on July 16, 2025, when he went to an immigration check-in.

Suárez had been ordered removed from the U.S. in 2000 after serving a prison sentence stemming from a plea agreement on a drug charge. Because Cuba was not accepting U.S. deportees then, Suárez was released and told to check in with ICE annually, a court document states. Cuba has allowed few of its citizens to return after U.S. deportation.

An attorney attempted to get Suárez released from detention. The federal judge had given DHS until late January to remove him or release him, but the judge then extended the government’s time for two weeks. On the deadline date, Feb. 11, DHS deported Suárez to Mexico and the judge closed the case.

“Forty-seven years. They took me to the U.S. as a 12-year-old, when I was a child,” Suárez said. “I was raised my whole life there [in the U.S.]. I’m bilingual and everything. I went to school there and everything. And everything happened from one moment to the next. I still can’t absorb what happened.”

Suárez said he had been a truck driver since he was 17 and had built his own truck driving business with his brother, an American citizen, who died in 2021 from Covid. His father had died in Cuba when he was 3 and his mother, who became a U.S. citizen, died about a decade ago.

When immigration laws were toughened in 1996, making legal residents deportable for certain crimes, he could no longer seek U.S. citizenship, he said.

His mother had urged him to get citizenship, but he didn’t do it, he said.

“I was pretty young. When you are pretty young, you don’t listen to anybody,” he said. He had no other encounters with law enforcement, he said. He said he’d been living a normal life, preparing to buy a house and had a girlfriend.

“Life is changed. I don’t know what is going to happen here in Mexico.”

title: Trump-backed congresswoman criticizes his immigration policies
description: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-FL) talks to reporters following a House Republican conference in the basement of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C.
fullText:
Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican up for re-election in November, released an ad on Thursday in which she criticized President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, just months after he endorsed her campaign.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in the ad. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

"You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism," she continued. "I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land. And only you can do that.”

The video marked a stunning break from the President who backed Salazar’s re-election bid earlier this year. In February, Trump said in a Truth Social post that the Congresswoman was “doing a truly fantastic job representing the wonderful people of Florida’s 27th Congressional District!” and that she “knows the Wisdom and Courage required to confront the Corrupt Fake News.” He said that she had his “Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election” before telling voters that Salazar “WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”

Salazar joins a growing number of Republicans who have publicly pushed back on Trump’s policies.

Trump has railed against other members of his party who have broken with him, going so far as to endorse several of their challengers in the primaries. The President endorsed Ed Gallrein, for instance, who ultimately defeated Rep. Thomas Massie in the May Republican primary for the Kentucky Congressman’s seat, after Massie broke with Trump on various issues, including objecting to the “One Big Beautiful Bill” and leading the effort to push the Department of Justice to release the so-called “Epstein files.”

Salazar’s campaign said that the video released on Thursday is the first of multiple ads that it plans to run before the upcoming midterm elections, in which Salazar is facing off against Democratic nominee Eliott Rodríguez. Both Salazar and Rodríguez are Cuban American, and previously worked as journalists.

Rodríguez criticized Salazar for the ad in a video that he shared on social media on Thursday, claiming that she had "desperately sought Donald Trump's endorsement" but was now speaking out "because [Trump's] immigration policy is political poison in her re-election campaign." Rodríguez went on to accuse his Republican opponent of being a "pathetic rubber stamp for Donald Trump."
"María Elvira Salazar did this—make no mistake about it," Rodríguez said. "She owns all of these deportations, ICE harassment, family separations, and racial profiling. She voted for it. She gave Donald Trump the money and the tools to do it. Now, just 47 days before the midterm election, she is trying to convince voters that she disagrees with Trump's inhumane practices on undocumented people with no criminal record."

The Cook Political Report indicates that Salazar, a three-term Congresswoman, is expected to hold on to her seat come November, rating it as “Likely Republican.”

In the district Salazar represents, the foreign-born population makes up more than 54% of the total population—one of the largest proportions of all the districts in the lower chamber.

Thursday’s ad isn’t the first time that Salazar has expressed concerns about the Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement efforts. Earlier this week, she responded to reports that Luis Galeano, an exiled Nicaraguan journalist whose U.S. asylum application has been pending for years, had been detained by federal immigration agents.

“America must always know the difference between a criminal and a political exile,” Salazar said in a statement shared on social media. “Luis is a respected journalist who paid a price for telling the truth about the Ortega-Murillo dictatorship. The regime persecuted him, forced him into exile, and stripped him of his citizenship. That history matters. He cannot be sent back into the hands of the people who targeted him.”

“I have been clear with the Administration: enforce the law and deport dangerous individuals, but do not treat political exiles like criminals,” she continued.

Salazar has also been backing a bipartisan measure in the House that would grant immigrants who don’t have a criminal history a route to secure legal status in the U.S., but not a pathway to citizenship.

title: Why Ohio State landed Deng Ngor before Duke, Florida could host visits
description: Ohio State landed a commitment from a top-20 forward when Deng Ngor picked the Buckeyes. Here's how they beat out Duke, Florida and others for him.
fullText:
On a different timeline, Deng Ngor and his family would have been on a plane headed west. For the weekend of Sept. 18, the four-star forward in the class of 2027 was scheduled to be on an official visit to Washington, one of three remaining such trips on his calendar.

After the Huskies, official visits Florida and Duke loomed for Ngor, a fast-rising prospect who added a host of high-major scholarship offers during the late spring and summer. There was just one problem, however: he'd already taken an official visit to Ohio State during the weekend of Sept. 4.

It was Ngor's first visit, and it proved to be the only one he needed. On Sept. 17, the 6-foot-8, 200-pound Canadian forward from Fort Erie (Ontario) International Academy publicly announced his commitment to the Buckeyes, passing on chances to check out his other three finalists.

"We were supposed to visit other big schools like Duke, but for our family it really felt right," said Joseph Ngor, Deng's father. "Security, academic support, small city, the community, the way we were treated there, there was nothing hidden from us, really."

Leading into the Ohio State visit, Joseph Ngor said the family had been doing research on the program to better understand what the situation might be like once they got there. Included in that work was the continual relationship-building between the Ngors and the Ohio State coaching staff since the Buckeyes offered him a scholarship May 28. The Huskies, Gators and Blue Devils would all eventually follow suit, but Ohio State assistant coach Luke Simons quickly established a bond with the family that steadily grew leading into the visit.

All of that came together on the official visit, Joseph Ngor said.

"The coaches, we dined with their families," he said. "As parents, that's what we were looking for, and my kid thinks his career will really excel where he's free. (Ohio State) gave him everything. He's the main guy (they're recruiting) at his position and everything seemed right, so instead of looking for other things we just said no and closed everything up.

"Luke is really great at connecting to the families. He's made a relationship far more than basketball."

When Ngor landed his Ohio State offer, he was unranked in the 247Sports.com database. After a strong spring and summer playing both AAU basketball and for Canada's U18 team, he has climbed to No. 55 in the class of 2027 according to the website. Rivals.com, in its most recent rankings refresh, moved him up to No. 19 nationally.

According to Neilball.com, Deng Ngor has played in 44 games between his high school and the AAU circuit in the past year and averaged 9.9 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.5 assists per game while shooting 52.8% from the field and 30.2% from 3-point range. During the spring and summer, he shot 34% from 3-point range while playing on the adidas circuit.

Ohio State Buckeyes: Value of joy instilled in Ohio State basketball's Amare Bynum from a young age

While helping Canada win a gold medal at the FIBA U18 AmeriCup, Deng Ngor averaged 10.2 points, 4.0 rebounds and 3.0 assists while shooting 37.5% (6 for 16) from 3-point range.

At Ohio State, Joseph Ngor said the coaches view him as a likely replacement for five-star freshman forward Anthony Thompson, who is widely projected as a first-round NBA draft prospect.

"He's a wing and a free shooter," he said. "The guy that's playing there now is projected to go to the NBA. That's what Jake (Diebler) was telling me, and so they said that he's the main guy for (them). His style of play fits their program, so they're going to adjust some things but he's going to play his style because that's (also) Ohio State's style."

Once the returned home from their Ohio State visit, Joseph Ngor said it felt like just a matter of time before they would commit to the Buckeyes.

"From the first day we visited, we left on (Sept. 6) and we were positive that is the one we were looking for," Joseph Ngor said. "We were talking to those (other) coaches who really wanted us to consider them. We were telling them positive things about our visit and they were saying, 'You're going to see that when you get to our campus. It's going to be pretty much the same, if not better.'

"I had some mixed feelings like, maybe we should just visit all of these schools and pick one later. Then the other part of me said if you do that, you're going to get more confused."

title: Former Florida Panthers Captain and Staffer Is Latest to Join Devils Front Office
description: FORT LAUDERDALE — Bryan McCabe left the Florida Panthers front office earlier this summer. On Wednesday, the team’s former captain officially […]
fullText:
FORT LAUDERDALE — Bryan McCabe left the Florida Panthers front office earlier this summer. On Wednesday, the team's former captain officially landed with the New Jersey Devils.

McCabe is the latest Florida front-office member to join the Devils since the end of last season.

New GM Sunny Mehta was one of Bill Zito's most trusted advisors; he brought Braden Birch, one of the Florida's top cap managers, with him.

"It's really hard to replace people, but it's a good thing where, hopefully, other folks will want to come thinking that 'hey, maybe I can get a chance to grow and expand my opportunities'," Bill Zito said on Wednesday.

"It's part of our game, and it's part of what we're all about. We want everyone to be successful and happy. They move along. Players do. I did. … It's a positive thing."

McCabe, who is now the Devils' VP of Prospect Personnel and Assistant General Manager of the AHL Utica Comets, spent the past 14 seasons with the Panthers in various player development roles.

A defenseman who played 15 seasons in the NHL, McCabe was traded to the Panthers in 2008 from the Toronto Maple Leafs after he had already played from the New York Islanders, Vancouver Canucks, and Chicago Blackhawks.

McCabe spent parts of three seasons with Florida and was named captain in 2009-10.

He ended his career in 2011 with the New York Rangers after scoring 145 goals with 528 points in 1,135 games.

In 2024, he finally became a Stanley Cup champion with the Panthers.

"To be part of it, it has obviously been a long time coming,'' McCabe said not long after Florida won its first championship.

"My first NHL game was 29 years [ago], so, yeah, a dream come true just to be a part of this whole thing with this group. This organization, making my home here, it has been very special.''

title: Maurkice Pouncey, Emmitt Smith to be inducted into Florida-Georgia Hall of Fame
description: Florida football greats Emmitt Smith, Maurkice Pouncey among those to be honored at Florida-Georgia rivalry game.
fullText:
Maurkice Pouncey and Emmitt Smith will be inducted into the Florida-Georgia Hall of Fame on Friday, Oct. 30.

The Florida football greats will be inducted at 12 p.m. at the Chick-fil-A College Football Hall of Fame in Atlanta. Former Georgia standouts Brandon Boykin and Andre Hastings will also be inducted.

This year's rivalry game will not be played in Jacksonville for the first time since 1995 due to stadium renovations. This season, the game will be played in Atlanta, while the following year will be hosted in Tampa in 2027 before returning to Jacksonville in 2028.

Before Smith became the NFL's all-time leading rusher, he rewrote the history books at Florida. From 1987 to 1989, the running back finished his career as the school's all-time leading rusher with 3,928 yards and 36 rushing touchdowns.

Pouncey was a member of the Gators from 2007-09, including a three-season run in which UF posted a 36-5 record, two SEC titles, and the 2008 BCS national championship.

The consensus All-American and future 18th overall pick of the NFL Draft started in 39 games for the Gators. In the NFL, Pouncey earned 9 Pro Bowl selections over an 11-year career.

title: Fourth Florida resident dies after contracting flesh-eating bacteria linked to oysters
description: Florida reports fourth Vibrio vulnificus death in 2026 as health officials warn about raw oysters, contaminated water and severe infections.
fullText:
A fourth person in Florida has died after contracting flesh-eating bacteria commonly linked to consuming raw or undercooked oysters, health officials said.

The death was included Thursday in the Florida Department of Health's updated fatality count for the deadly flesh-eating bacterium Vibrio vulnificus.

The individual was from Broward County and between the ages of 75 and 79, WSFA reported. It remains unclear exactly how the person contracted the infection.

Previous deaths were attributed to residents of Bay, Palm Beach and Marion counties, according to the state's health department.

Beachgoers Warned After Deadly 'Flesh-eating' Bacteria Kills 5 In Southern State

"Most people get vibriosis by eating raw or undercooked shellfish, particularly oysters," the Florida Department of Health said.

According to the department's website, Florida has reported 21 cases of Vibrio vulnificus in 2026.

In the last 10 years, 2022 and 2024 reported some of the highest numbers of cases and deaths in the region. Florida recorded 19 deaths and 82 cases in 2024, while 2022 saw 17 deaths and 74 cases.

North Carolina Mountain Community Braces For Hurricane Season Two Years After Helene's Brutal Impact

Officials said the unusual increase stemmed from certain counties experiencing impacts from hurricanes Helene and Ian. Severe weather events that cause standing or floodwaters pose a risk of exposure to the bacteria, officials said.

Vibrio vulnificus is a naturally occurring bacterium found in warm, brackish seawater.

Popular Beaches Closed As High Bacteria Levels Raise Health Concerns For Swimmers

Exposure can occur when a person eats oysters contaminated with the bacteria or enters contaminated water with an open wound.

Health officials said bloodstream infections caused by Vibrio vulnificus are fatal about 50% of the time.

While healthy individuals typically develop a mild illness, Vibrio vulnificus infections can cause severe illness in people with weakened immune systems.

"A recent study showed that people with these pre-existing medical conditions were 80 times more likely to develop Vibrio vulnificus bloodstream infections than healthy people," Florida health officials said.

'I Thought I Had The Flu': Mom Nearly Died After Dismissing Deadly Sepsis Symptoms

Severe infections can cause symptoms including fever, chills, decreased blood pressure, also known as septic shock, and blistering skin lesions. In some cases, wound infections can lead to tissue damage requiring amputation.

Elsewhere along the Gulf Coast, Louisiana has reported 15 cases and six deaths this year as of Sept. 9, according to the Louisiana Department of Health. Fourteen of the cases were attributed to wound or seawater exposure.

The Texas Department of State Health Services says Texas typically sees an average of 33 cases per year.

Mississippi reported three cases as of August, according to the state's health department.

title: A Florida investor explains how he bought 3 condos for $360,000 and turned them into cash-flowing rentals using the 1% rule
description: Ted Garber broadened his search for cash flowing properties when he couldn't find what he wanted closer to home. He shares the numbers behind one deal.
fullText:
Florida-based investor Ted Garber walks Business Insider through one of his deals.

He bought a 3-condo portfolio for $360,000 in 2022.

He shares how he financed it and turned it into a cash-flowing asset.

Ted Garber did not set out to become a long-distance landlord, but after struggling to find the cash flow he wanted close to home, he broadened his search.

Looking at neighboring counties "really opened up the opportunities for us," the part-time investor, who has built a portfolio of Florida rentals alongside his wife, Jamie, told Business Insider.

In September 2022, the Garbers bought three occupied condos listed together for $360,000. The properties were about a 90-minute drive from their Florida home. It was their first out-of-area acquisition — and an experiment to see whether they could self-manage rentals without being on-site regularly.

Four years later, Garber said they have visited the properties just once and spend less than an hour a week managing their broader portfolio of 29 tenants.

He opened the books on the deal and shared how he picked the condos, financed the purchase, and turned the portfolio into a cash-flowing asset. BI verified the purchase and the Garbers' ownership of the three condos by reviewing the final ALTA Settlement Statement and new landlord letters showing the rent for each unit.

Garber found the three-condo portfolio on LoopNet, where the listed gross rent immediately caught his attention. At the $360,000 purchase price, the condos generated $3,675 in combined monthly rent, just over 1% of the price.

That satisfied Garber's initial screening tool: the 1% rule. The rule of thumb suggests that a property's monthly rent should be at least 1% of its purchase price to have a reasonable chance of generating positive cash flow. It is not a guarantee, but it is a quick way to decide whether a listing is worth investigating further.

He also saw room to increase rents, which he determined were below market, and liked the stable area outside Orlando's Disney corridor.

To make the numbers work, however, he had to negotiate. The condo portfolio was initially listed for between $390,000 and $400,000, he said.

That's a typical step in his process, he added: "I always negotiate. If it's really a steal, I'll do full asking immediately with a seller concession or something."

Before making an offer, Garber makes sure his financing is in place. In this case, the couple financed the purchase with a commercial loan amortized over 20 years at an interest rate of roughly 5.5%.

title: Social media reacts to Florida's Week 2 blowout of Campbell
description: Get a gander at how the Gator Nation is reacting to Florida football's Week 2 bludgeoning of the Campbell Fighting Camels in the Swamp on Saturday.

title: No. 18 FSU soccer ties NC State 2-2 in ACC opener
description: No. 18 Florida State hosted NC State Friday evening in its first ACC matchup of the season, ending the night with a 2-2 draw. The Seminoles move to 4-1-2 on the season, while the Wolfpack move to 7-0-2. FSU goalkeeper Kate Ockene entered the matchup after being named ACC Goalkeeper of the Week for her […]
fullText:
No. 18 Florida State hosted NC State Friday evening in its first ACC matchup of the season, ending the night with a 2-2 draw.

The Seminoles move to 4-1-2 on the season, while the Wolfpack move to 7-0-2.

FSU goalkeeper Kate Ockene entered the matchup after being named ACC Goalkeeper of the Week for her performance against Rice on Sunday.

Florida State's starting lineup featured Ockene in goal; Olivia Page and Claire Rain on the back line; Shaneil Buckley, Peyton McGovern, Joelle Jung and Sam Erbach in the midfield; and Nyah Rose, Tanner Strickland, Wrianna Hudson and Ryder Ajeto up front.

The Seminoles were still without Bridget Mutipula, Janet Okeke and Nyanya Touray, who are competing in the FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup.

NC State wasted little time getting on the board. Erica Roberts scored just 1:37 into the match to give the Wolfpack an early 1-0 lead.

FSU continued looking for opportunities to answer, and the Seminoles found one in the 22nd minute. Buckley sent the ball to Hudson in front of the goal, where Hudson headed it into the net to tie the match at 1-1.

Use that height, Wri!! 😤 pic.twitter.com/W0Ah7Rrig1

The Seminoles continued looking for another opportunity before halftime. Erbach took a free kick from outside the 18-yard box that found Hudson, but her header was saved by NC State goalkeeper Riley Pickels.

At 41:42, Erbach had another opportunity, but her shot went just over the goal.

NC State entered halftime with seven shots compared to FSU's two. The physicality also started to show, with the Wolfpack recording four fouls and a yellow card, while the Seminoles had two fouls.

The Wolfpack regained the lead at 57:32 when sophomore Daisy Duda found the back of the net to make it 2-1.

Once again, the Seminoles had to find an answer.

At 64:29, Buckley stayed persistent in front of the goal and finished the opportunity, tying the match at 2-2.

What a pretty-placed shot by Prinny! 👑 pic.twitter.com/u2yRenKOdZ

Neither team was able to find the go-ahead goal, leaving FSU with a draw in its first ACC matchup of the season.

NC State finished the match with 13 shots, four on goal, while FSU recorded seven shots, five on goal. The Wolfpack also held an advantage in corner kicks, having eight and FSU having none. NC State finished with 12 fouls compared to six for Florida State.

Head coach Brian Pensky and the Seminoles now have more than a week away from competition to regroup, watch film and continue working on their chemistry as a team.

Florida State will return to ACC play on Sept. 27, traveling to Louisville for its second noon matchup of the season.

title: Innocent woman says police use of Flock camera led to 13 days in jail
description: Lindsey Brooke Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after a Flock camera flagged her Dodge Durango near a fatal Florida crash that killed three people.
fullText:
Lindsey Brooke Isaacs was asleep at home when police arrived and told the 23-year-old that her car had been involved in a crash that killed three people. She knew they had the wrong person. Her black Dodge Durango showed no obvious collision damage, and she had a receipt showing where she had been.

Still, the investigation eventually led to her being arrested and 13 days in jail. "My heart was in my stomach," Lindsey told me on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/. "I didn't know what was going on."

Months later, prosecutors dropped all eight felony charges against her and investigators arrested another woman in connection with the crash. Her case now raises a bigger question about how much weight investigators should give license plate camera data when a person's freedom is on the line.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You'll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

License Plate Cameras Are Tracking Drivers Everywhere

The deadly crash happened on Oct. 4, 2025, along eastbound Interstate 4 near DeBary, Florida. Motorcyclist Joaquin Deno died. Flagler County Deputy Administrator Jorge Salinas and his wife, Nancy Salinas, also died. Witnesses reported that a Dodge Durango was involved.

Investigators found Lindsey's black Dodge Durango through a Flock automated license plate reader. The camera recorded her vehicle traveling eastbound near the Seminole and Volusia county line at 9:51 p.m. That camera was about three miles west of the crash scene. The crash happened around 9:53 p.m. That timing became especially important later.

Lindsey's attorney, Patrick McGeehan, said his team performed a time-distance analysis and concluded Lindsey was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. So the camera really did capture Lindsey's vehicle. The problem came from what investigators concluded from that sighting. Lindsey put it more bluntly during our conversation. "They just picked up my car off a camera and called it the end of the day. We got her."

The Flock camera hit was far from the only information investigators had. A 911 caller described a maroon Dodge Durango and provided part of its license plate number. Later, investigators also found red or maroon paint transfer on a Ford Focus involved in the crash.

Meanwhile, Lindsey drove a black Dodge Durango. A specialized Florida Highway Patrol team later inspected Lindsey's vehicle and reported finding no damage suggesting it had been involved in a collision with another vehicle.

That finding lined up with something Lindsey said she had been telling investigators from the beginning. "Where is the damage on the vehicle?" she recalled asking police. "Because I'm standing right in front of it and I don't see any damage." Still, authorities impounded her SUV. Months passed.

On April 17, 2026, Lindsey got a call from her attorney. She had to surrender that day. "They are arresting you for this crime," Lindsey recalled him telling her. She faced eight felony charges: three counts of vehicular homicide, three counts of leaving the scene of a crash involving death, leaving the scene involving serious bodily injury and reckless driving causing serious bodily injury. Lindsey spent 13 days in jail.

During our podcast conversation, she described spending her first several days in solitary confinement. She said she had a toilet, a sink and a metal sleeping slab covered by a thin mat. Her charges were so serious, she said, that jail officials initially kept her separated from other people.

Later, Lindsey was transferred to other sections of the jail. After her first bond hearing, she remained behind bars. "I was devastated, I was scared," she told me. "I thought my life was over."

How Surveillance Tech Led Police To Accuse The Wrong Person

A new investigation changes the case

The case finally began moving in a very different direction after prosecutors and a specialized Florida Highway Patrol team took another look. That team found no meaningful crash damage on Lindsey's Durango. Investigators revisited witness information and followed evidence pointing toward another vehicle.

On May 22, the State Attorney's Office formally declined to prosecute Lindsey on all eight charges. Authorities then arrested Alisa Lee Montalvo on charges connected to the crash. Prosecutors allege Montalvo was driving a maroon Dodge Durango. She faces nine charges, including three counts of vehicular homicide and tampering with physical evidence. She has not been convicted, and the charges remain allegations.

For Lindsey, the news brought enormous relief. "I felt like a new woman," she told me. "I felt free." Lindsey told me she later received an apology from the head of the Florida Highway Patrol. "It felt like a miracle," she said. "Another miracle from God that I was hearing it in person, face to face."

However, she also said the experience left lasting emotional and physical effects. "This took and is going to take maybe years to get better mentally, physically, emotionally," Lindsey said. Lindsey has since filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against two Florida Highway Patrol troopers involved in the investigation, alleging false arrest, wrongful imprisonment and malicious prosecution. Those claims have not been proven in court.

We reached out to Flock Safety and the Florida Highway Patrol for comment. Flock Safety responded with the following statement:

"Flock cameras provide investigative leads; they do not identify perpetrators, determine guilt, or make arrest decisions. In fact, the complaint itself calls the Flock evidence 'exculpatory, not inculpatory,' meaning the evidence pointed away from Ms. Isaacs rather than implicating her: it accurately placed her vehicle three miles from the crash scene just two minutes before the crash. Characterizing her arrest as the result of Flock technology fundamentally misrepresents both the allegations and the role our technology played in this case."

The Florida Highway Patrol did not respond to our request for comment.

Flock cameras are automated license plate readers, often called ALPRs. They capture images of passing vehicles and use software to identify license plates. Flock systems can also capture vehicle characteristics including make, model and color. Each camera sighting can create a record linking a vehicle with a particular place and time.

For police, that can become an extremely useful investigative tool. A stolen car can appear on a camera. A vehicle connected to a missing person case could produce a lead. However, Lindsey's experience raises another question. What happens when investigators put too much confidence in one search result? We previously explored that concern after surveillance technology helped police accuse a Colorado woman of stealing a package. Her own phone location history eventually helped show where she had really been.

One of the most interesting moments in my conversation with Lindsey came when I asked whether she blamed the Flock technology or the way police interpreted its data. Her answer was clear. "I 100% think the second one you said, how police interpret the camera footage," she told me. That gets to the heart of this story.

The Flock camera captured Lindsey's vehicle traveling on I-4. The machine did what it was designed to do. Human judgment came next. Investigators had to decide what that sighting meant. They also had to weigh it against witness accounts, physical evidence and the condition of Lindsey's car.

According to Lindsey's federal complaint, the Flock hit three miles from the crash two minutes beforehand, ultimately helped her legal team argue that she was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. Technology can surface a lead. People still have to prove what that lead actually means.

Flock Safety Cameras Need Constitutional Guardrails Before Further Deployment, Tennessee Mayor Argues

The debate over these cameras has now taken a major turn in Florida. On Aug. 31, the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for license plate reader systems within rights-of-way on Florida's state highway system.

FDOT cited the rapid growth of the systems along with reports of misuse and concerns involving data privacy and surveillance. Cameras covered by the order must be removed within 30 days. The agency also said it will stop issuing future permits for license plate readers within its jurisdiction.

However, that order does not eliminate every Flock camera in Florida. It applies to cameras within FDOT-controlled state highway rights of way. Local governments can take different approaches to cameras on city or county property. Several agencies have chosen to pull back further. Miami-Dade County, for example, announced that it would suspend its entire license plate reader program. Other Florida agencies plan to continue using cameras away from state highways.

Flock Safety has also announced significant changes to how its system operates. In August, the company announced that it was changing its recommended and default license plate data retention period from 30 days to seven days.

Flock also plans to require law enforcement customers to use its Audit Assistance tool by the end of 2026. The technology flags unusual search activity for review.

Case codes will also become mandatory for law enforcement searches by the end of the year. Flock says emergency searches can bypass that requirement, although those searches will be flagged for review. Those changes add oversight. Still, safeguards inside the software cannot determine whether an investigator has drawn the right conclusion from the information on the screen.

Most of us probably drive past license plate readers without noticing them. A single plate scan may seem harmless. After all, anyone standing beside the road can see your license plate.

A searchable network changes the equation. Instead of someone seeing your vehicle once, a network of cameras can record when that vehicle passed particular locations.

We have already reported on Flock license plate cameras appearing at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots. We also reported on a Washington court ruling that found Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records under that state's Public Records Act.

Lindsey told me she knew Flock cameras existed before her ordeal. She simply had no idea how much could ride on the information they collected. "I just thought it was like a traffic camera," she said. Today, her opinion has changed. "I feel very different about those cameras now."

Powerful Crime-fighting Surveillance Growth Spurs Lawmakers To Issue Warning: 'Orwellian'

If police tell you that your vehicle appeared in a license plate reader search tied to a serious crime, your own records could become important.

Save receipts and toll records that can help establish where you were. If your phone already stores location history, preserve that information too. Avoid changing or deleting anything related to the period investigators are asking about.

Doorbell cameras and security systems often overwrite older recordings. If footage could show your vehicle at home or somewhere else, preserve a copy as soon as possible. The same goes for dashcam video.

If authorities claim your car was involved in a collision, take detailed pictures and video showing its condition. Photograph and record each side of the vehicle and keep the original files with their date information intact.

A serious criminal accusation can escalate quickly. An attorney can help preserve evidence and communicate with investigators. Legal counsel can also examine whether the available data actually supports what police believe happened.

I'm torn on Flock cameras. If somebody burglarizes my home, I want police to have technology that can help identify the vehicle that drove away. If investigators are trying to locate a missing person, a license plate reader could provide a valuable lead. But Lindsey's story shows what can happen when a lead begins driving the investigation instead of helping investigators test what really happened. Her black Dodge Durango had no crash damage. Other evidence pointed toward a maroon Durango. The timing of the Flock hit ultimately helped her attorney argue that she could not have caused the crash. Yet she still spent 13 days in jail. As I told Lindsey during our conversation, "I can't stand when technology is used in ways that it was never intended for." That is where I land on this. The technology can be incredibly useful. The people using it still need to challenge what they think they know before someone loses their freedom. For more of Lindsey's remarkable firsthand account, listen to or watch my full conversation with her on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/.

After hearing what happened to Lindsey, would you want Flock cameras in your community, or has this case changed how you feel about police tracking license plates? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Florida woman accused of DUI crashes SUV into parked car, then makes bizarre plea to police caught on camera
description: Surveillance video allegedly shows a Florida woman smashing into a parked car in Daytona Beach before she pleaded with police officers not to take her to jail.
fullText:
A Florida woman accused of plowing an SUV into a parked car appeared to downplay the collision before making a personal plea to officers investigating her, newly released video shows.

"I thought we were all friends," 24-year-old Elizabeth Boucher told Daytona Beach police during the Aug. 30 encounter.

Surveillance video released by police shows an SUV smashing into a parked Honda with enough force to shove it across a front lawn and out of the camera's view.

But when an officer asked Boucher what happened, she offered a far less dramatic account caught on police bodycam video.

Bodycam Shows Nantucket Official Slurring, Swaying During Dui Stop After Crashing Into Sign: Police

"I guess I hit the front light of those cars, but I don't know what really happened," Boucher said.

"You didn't just hit the front of the car," the officer fired back. "You just took the car completely off."

Body camera video shows the officer then asking Boucher for her driver's license. She instead hands him a passport.

Bodycam Video Shows Canadian Woman Allegedly Giving False Name Before Deputies Discovered 12 Fake Ids

"That's a passport," he tells her before again asking for her license.

As the roadside investigation unfolded, Boucher pleaded with officers not to lock her up.

"It's just a vape. I know. It didn't even work," she said. "Please don't take me to jail over this."

An officer later told Boucher the case had been shifted from a civil crash investigation to a criminal DUI investigation and read her Miranda rights.

Asked whether she would perform field sobriety exercises, Boucher refused, according to the video. She also declined a breath test after an officer formally requested one.

Repeat Drunken-driving Offender Accused Of Killing Honors College Student Heading Home From Wedding

When Boucher again invoked their supposed friendship, an officer responded, "But we still have a job to do."

"I know. I'm not resisting arrest," Boucher said. "I just want to make sure my daughter gets what she needs."

An officer then instructed her to lean against a vehicle "so you don't fall."

"Am I going to jail?" Boucher asked moments later.

The woman whose vehicle was struck also told officers that Boucher had confronted and slapped her after the crash, according to the bodycam video.

Suspected Drunk Driver Kills 2 Pedestrians In Violent Chain-reaction Crash On Manhattan's Upper West Side

"Did she touch you at any point?" an officer asked.

"Yeah, she smacked me right here," the woman alleges before saying she wanted to press charges.

After she was placed under arrest, Boucher appeared confused by the slow-moving process.

"Why am I sitting here all alone? Why is nothing happening?" she asked.

"That's normally what happens when you are arrested," an officer told her.

Boucher was charged with driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, DUI involving damage to property or another person, refusing to submit to DUI testing, battery by touching or striking, resisting an officer without violence and possessing a controlled substance without a prescription, according to police.

An attorney for Boucher could not immediately be identified.

She was released from jail Aug. 31 and has pleaded not guilty to the charges, according to court records.

She is expected back in court in October.

title: Dangerous mosquito-borne virus spreads in one state as officials warn of rising cases
description: Florida dengue fever cases hit 41 statewide as mosquito-control crews ramp up aerial spraying and inspections across Tampa Bay's hardest-hit counties.
fullText:
Florida mosquito-control agencies are stepping up surveillance, inspections and spraying, as officials expect the number of locally acquired dengue fever cases in Tampa Bay and across the state to rise in the coming weeks.

As of Sept. 1, the number of dengue fever cases originating in Florida this year had climbed to 33 in Tampa Bay and 41 statewide. Cases are predicted to increase, Fox 13 Tampa Bay reported.

Locally acquired cases mean people contracted the illness where they live rather than while traveling abroad.

Deadly Mosquito-borne Virus Claims First Life In Major Us City As Cases Spread

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) reported 30 confirmed cases in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County.

Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts issued by the Florida Department of Health.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The virus is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.

Hawaii has recorded past outbreaks, and the virus is common in the U.S. territories of Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and American Samoa.

The CDC reported in May that 2024 was a record year for dengue in the U.S.

A total of 3,798 cases were reported from U.S. states and the District of Columbia, a 359% increase over the annual average for 2010 through 2023. About 97% of those cases were travel-associated, and roughly 3% were locally acquired.

Florida reported the most dengue cases among U.S. states and Washington, D.C., in 2024, with 1,044 cases, or more than a quarter of the total. Florida recorded 85 locally acquired cases across 10 counties that year, compared with 18 in California and two in Texas.

Test Yourself With Our Latest Lifestyle Quiz

"Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro told Fox 13.

"The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day. When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission."

Mosquito-control crews in Florida are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to local reports.

FMCA is urging residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.

The FMCA also advises people to follow what it calls the "three Ds."

Dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.

Defend with a repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus.

Dump standing water from containers around the home, and check yards regularly.

Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic.

In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness.

People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

title: Florida AG seeks death penalty for couple who allegedly held 4 children in ‘rolling prison’ for over 6 years
description: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier says his office will seek the death penalty for two adults who allegedly confined four children to a truck cab.
fullText:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier says his office will seek the death penalty for the two adults who allegedly confined four children to the cab of a tractor-trailer, some for more than six years, and sexually abused them.

Keisha Monique Epps, 51, and Tamra Marshon Stewart, 37, have been charged with sexual battery, molestation and neglect of two girls and two boys — two 5-year-olds, a 6-year-old and a 9-year-old, Uthmeier said.

Epps and Stewart, who has been identified as her fiancé, had been living in the cab with the children. Epps worked as a truck driver, frequenting a route between Miami and Atlanta, according to court documents.

Florida Couple Allegedly Held Four Children In Tractor-trailer Cab For Nearly Seven Years

"These children were trapped in a rolling prison and abused by the adults who were supposed to protect them," Uthmeier said.

"We will pursue with everything we have the death penalty. We will seek executions, if you want to come in here [in Florida] and you want to physically molest, abuse, and violate our little kids."

Florida law allows prosecutors to seek the death penalty for adults convicted of sexual battery against a child younger than 12.

The two girls were sexually abused by Stewart for years, Uthmeier said. When the two boys witnessed sexual abuse and confronted Stewart, he "beat them by punching them in their heads," reports show.

The children told authorities that they had told Epps about the sexual abuse and saw her witness it. She called one of the children "derogatory names" and continued to leave them alone with Stewart, reports show.

Stewart told investigators he had committed three sexual batteries against one of the girls, according to Uthmeier's office.

One of the children was found to have an untreated sexually transmitted infection, Uthmeier's office said.

But the horrors allegedly went far beyond sexual abuse.

The couple confined the children in the truck cab without "time to take showers, use the restroom" or "exercise outside," investigators wrote in their reports.

"This case is one of, if not the most, horrific that my team has ever had to work on," Uthmeier said at a news conference in Kissimmee, Florida, on Sept. 1.

Over the years of their imprisonment, the children were forced to "use the bathroom" in cups and paper bags, he said. When making stops, "the adults would go to the restroom," Uthmeier said. "They might take a shower, but they would leave the kids locked in this rolling dungeon."

"As a result of the abuse" over the years, he said, the children "suffer severe physical infirmities."

The children were kept inside the vehicle "for the majority of their days," court records show.

The children said they hadn't been "allowed to attend school for approximately five years," according to an arrest report. A detective on the case reported the children were "walking with an unnatural gait from being confined to the cab."

They were "fed poorly," and they never received medical or dental care—even for emergencies, the report shows.

Two of the children suffered untreated burns that left significant scarring, according to Uthmeier's office.

One of the girls recalled a time she "burned herself badly with cooked noodles."

"There was a lot of blood," the girl told investigators.

Neither Stewart nor Epps took her to get medical treatment, she told investigators. Now, she has a "permanent scar" from the burn, court records show.

Stewart was in charge of supervising the children when Epps was sleeping, showering and driving the truck, the children said.

All four shared a bunk in the cab so small that they had to lie "curled up side by side," reports show.

Stewart is charged with "two counts of sexual battery by a person in familial or custodial authority, two counts of lewd or lascivious molestation of a child under 12, two counts of battery of a child by expelling certain fluids or materials, two counts of child neglect without great bodily harm, and two counts of child neglect causing permanent disfigurement," according to Uthmeier's office.

Epps is charged with "two counts of sexual battery by a person in familial or custodial authority, two counts of lewd or lascivious molestation of a child under 12, two counts of child neglect without great bodily harm, two counts of child neglect causing permanent disfigurement, and four counts of failure to report child abuse."

These charges will be prosecuted in the Ninth Judicial Circuit, Uthmeier said.

Epps and Stewart were arrested on Aug. 6. On Sept. 3, both were held in the Duval County Jail.

The Duval County Office of the Public Defender is representing Stewart, and Epps is represented by Florida's Office of Criminal Conflict and Civil Regional Counsel.

Neither office responded to a request for comment before publication.

title: Florida State soccer ties Rice University 1-1 before ACC play
description: In their last pre-conference game, the Seminoles tied with Rice University 1-1 on Sept. 6 after Rice met the 'Noles' only goal in the last 10 minutes.
fullText:
The No. 15 Seminoles have started off the 2026 season 4-1-0, taking victories against the University of Stetson, Florida International University (FIU), Florida Atlantic University (FAU), but falling short to the University of Florida (UF).

Most recently, the Seminoles bounced back from the first loss of the season when it hit the road, bringing home a win against No. 25 University of Georgia (UGA) on Thursday, Sept. 3.

'Noles soccer continued their season on Sunday, Sept. 6 at noon against the Rice University Owls at the Seminole Soccer Complex. The match resulted in a draw, as it was the last non-conference game for the Garnet and Gold.

The match started out hot as junior forward Wrianna Hudson scored the first goal of the match just under two minutes in. The Owls began to pick things up with a shot that was saved by sophomore goalkeeper Kate Ockene eight minutes into the game.

As the first half continued, Florida State led in shots 6-5. The score remained 0-0 going into halftime. Six minutes into the second half, Ockene made yet again another save, this being her fourth. She finished with eight saves on the day.

"I mean, I'm a goalkeeper for a reason," Kate Ockene said in the postgame press conference. "I wanna show up for my team the best I can do because they show up for me"

Shortly after minute 75, Hudson broke the ice and scored, giving the Seminoles a 1-0 lead. Hudson headed the ball in off a corner kick from junior forward Sam Erbach, giving her a second goal of the 2026 season.

'Nole of the Week: FSU midfielder, forward Sam Erbach

Not long after Hudson's goal, Rice took advantage and swept in as freshman forward Sloane Popov scored at 81:30, tying the game at 1-1 with just under 10 minutes remaining in the match.

"We battled obviously," head coach Brian Pensky said in the postgame press conference. "The effort was good, we got a goal, we just unfortunately couldn't finish it out"

As the second half went on, FSU continued to fight and play strong. Freshman forward Ryder Ajeto gave the 'Noles a glimpse of hope, scoring at '84, but after a video review, the goal was disallowed.

"Obviously we have a new team, 16 new players, so every single game is just time and we keep growing from every single game. I think our defense is getting stronger and stronger every game it's just one of those things that takes time," Ockene said.

The Garnet and Gold continues to move forward in their season, while also making sure to bond together with the addition of 16 new players this season.

"On the field we are getting better and better," Ockene said. "I think we're super close together."

With non-conference play now behind them, Florida State now turns its attention to Atlantic Coastal Conference (ACC) play. The season continues for the Seminoles when they face North Carolina State this Friday Sept. 11. at home.

"I think we're ready to fight for each other Friday night against NC State," Pensky said.

title: Jon Sumrall praises offense, challenges defense after FAU win
description: Jon Sumrall discussed Aaron Philo's debut, Jadan Baugh's explosive performance and areas Florida must improve after its season-opening win over FAU.
fullText:
Florida football coach Jon Sumrall met with reporters following the Gators' season-opening win over FAU on Saturday night.

Sumrall evaluated Aaron Philo's debut as Florida's starting quarterback, Jadan Baugh's explosive performance and an offense that produced 66 points and 624 yards. He also praised Vernell Brown III, D.J. Coleman and the Gators' perimeter blocking.

The first-year Florida coach was less satisfied with his defense, saying the unit has plenty to correct despite the lopsided victory. Sumrall also discussed his first Gator Walk, running onto Florida Field and the importance of continuing to develop the team's younger players.

Here's everything Sumrall had to say.

Glad to be 1-0 and happy for our guys. It was fun watching a lot of our production tonight. I thought the guys came into the game with the right mindset and the right approach.

They were prepared. They didn't take the opportunity for granted. They were emotionally charged and ready to go. There is a lot to clean up. It was by no means a perfect performance. There is a long list of things we have to get a lot better at if we have high goals here.

I'm grateful for the fans. Unbelievable turnout and energy. It was electric. I got asked a little bit ago about running out of the tunnel for the first time. It surpassed my expectations, and I had pretty high expectations of what it was going to be like. What an unbelievable crowd and great support. They had a huge impact on the game. We need that each and every week, which I have no doubt we will.

I'm grateful for the guys' effort. There is a lot to work on and a lot to grow from. I told them just now that the journey of a thousand miles starts with a single step. That was step one. The goal this week was to be 1-0. We've got to go back to the drawing board and get a little bit better each day this week to keep improving.

I'm proud of him. He's prepared. He has worked really, really hard. He's an unbelievable teammate. He's a great leader. The game means a lot to him. I think he showed his comfortability by how he operated. He made good decisions for the most part with the football.

He was accurate. He distributed it well. I thought he did a really nice job. The interception really wasn't on him, to be quite honest with you. That ball should have been caught. I thought he played really well.

We're really young as a team. Jadan Baugh may not be young, but there were a lot of guys out there playing football who are just young.

I told the staff going into the game that we were going to be aggressive all night. We're not in any position to shut it down right now. We've got to figure out who the next guy up is and roll guys in. We weren't going to change how we played the game.

I'm very proud of Aaron. His preparation showed up tonight in how he played.

He had a little ankle injury. I don't know how severe it is. He tried to give it a go. We'll see. I'll probably have more information for y'all Monday. Unfortunately, it happened really, really early.

He's a really good football player. I tell Buster all the time, "Don't know what to do? Just hand it to 13. That will work, usually." He's phenomenal. He's a great kid and every bit as good as I thought he would be. I told him the night before the game, "Hey, I'm glad you're still here. Thanks for staying."

I'm very, very glad he's a Florida Gator. I love his playing style and demeanor. I also had a great appreciation for seeing his enthusiasm late in the game when he wasn't playing.

He was excited for his teammates to have opportunities and success when he saw Duke, Byron and some of the other guys in the room get carries. Rubio got in there. Seeing his excitement for his teammates says a lot about him, too.

Early on, we couldn't keep pace with them. Our defense was atrocious at times, quite honestly. We had a hard time keeping pace with them. I'll watch the tape, but I'm a little bit frustrated with how we played defensively at times.

I don't think we're as good as we think we are. I think we've got some guys who feel like we've arrived in some spots, and that will be addressed. We've got a lot of room to grow on defense.

If it doesn't happen really fast, we're going to get embarrassed and exposed pretty handily in some spots because that wasn't a great performance by us.

Hats off to FAU. They do some really good things. I love their quarterback. I played against the kid last year. I love the way he plays. He's tough, competitive and a leader. He's just a really good football player.

Zach does a great job offensively. Their offensive staff is really good at what it does, and they stress you out. That number eight, the little slot receiver, hit us on a slot fade. He's a good player. He averaged 12 targets a game last year for them. I'm sure he probably had about that tonight. I don't know how many he caught, but it felt like every time they threw to him, something good happened for them.

It was a good test. It was a really good test for a Week 1 game. They're a talented team, and I wish them nothing but the best.

It was a long day, but it was a great day. It was fun. A lot of fun. I tried to take in as much of it as I could, but at the end of the day, it's about winning a game. You're focused on what we've got to do to position ourselves to be successful on the field.

But all the great things around our program make this place what it is. The Gator Walk was unbelievable. When we left the hotel, there was a crowd of people in the hotel parking lot. I'm like, "All right, this is kind of cool. These people are waiting to see our guys walk to the bus at the hotel."

The support we have here is unbelievable, and I could not be more grateful for it. We're doing everything we can to make them proud. I'm very grateful for what Florida Gator Nation is all about.

It was fun. It was good. There was a lot of good in there and plenty of things to get better at. But I want our guys to have fun playing. I tell our team all the time that when you were growing up as a kid, you never said, "I want to go work football today." You always said, "I want to go play football." That doesn't mean it doesn't take hard work, but the work should be fun. Competing is fun, and making plays is fun.

The thing I'm most proud of tonight offensively is our perimeter blocking. Our receivers blocked their asses off. In the run game we created tonight, there were times on the perimeter when our receivers were competing to make blocks.

That says a lot about who they are. The character of a football player sometimes isn't revealed when he is getting opportunities for production. It's revealed by what he is doing to serve his team. I thought those guys blocked with edge and competitiveness.

That makes it fun. Competing is fun. I think it was a fun brand to watch tonight. We need to keep it up.

It was exhilarating. I was like, "All right, this is real." The energy in the stadium was — man, it was on fire. You could feel it. It was probably even better than I thought it was going to be. It was just really, really cool.

D.J. is one of those guys who is just really consistent. He's a high-level communicator. He has a high football IQ. He's smart, tough and dependable. I'm not surprised.

He showed it in the spring game. He had a pick on the glance route, and everybody was like, "Oh, the quarterback threw a pick." I'm like, "Well, that was a freaking unbelievable play that 33 made."

He's a really good player, and I'm glad he's on our football team. He has been a great pickup for us. He practices really hard every day. He invests a lot in his craft. He's just a steady, steady player. I'm not surprised by how he played because that's how he practices.

He had a big night. That was his first touchdown. I was getting on him all offseason. I'm like, "You haven't scored here. Everybody thinks you're this big-time player. We've got to see you score touchdowns."

To see him make the plays he made tonight — he had a couple of big plays. The first one was explosive. It was a great, great play by him. He's another unbelievable worker, so I'm not surprised. He competes his tail off and prepares the right way.

I'm happy for his success because he's one of the best leaders for a young player I've ever been around. He's a second-year player, a true sophomore, and he's a phenomenal leader and a great teammate.

That was good. He stuck his foot in the ground at the end of that run to get more and didn't just think the journey was over. I think he has taken on that challenge. We've challenged him with that sometimes on long, explosive runs.

I tell the receivers and the guys on the perimeter that an eight-, 10- or 12-yard run becomes a 40- or 50-yard run because they block better. They get on the safeties, and you're kind of nagging the defensive backs and getting in their way to create longer runs.

It was great to see him pop that long one. I'm proud of his performance.

Like I said, I thought our perimeter blocking was good. I thought certain guys on defense, at times, showed their contact courage. Maybe we weren't where we needed to be across the board, but I felt some physicality.

Procedurally, I'm probably most pleased with the offense. A lot of times in Game 1, there are delay-of-game penalties, illegal formations, false starts or a lot of other issues. It felt fairly clean in how we operated offensively.

Our special teams played really well. Durk hit the 50-plus-yarder. I think it was a 53-yarder. I thought he kicked the ball off well.

Other than the kickoff coverage where we missed a hit and didn't make the tackle, which I wasn't pleased with, I thought there were a lot of good areas.

At that point, I'm never going to be the one who tries to run up the score, per se. But I'm also not going to be someone who just shuts it down. Micah Jones scored the last touchdown, right? That was Micah, correct?

He is on the scout team all week right now. He's a young player who needs to improve for his own development and for our football team to continue growing. Byron Louis is kind of the fourth or fifth back right now, so I wanted to see him play.

I wanted to see Tramell operate and compete. I wanted to get Will Griffin in. If we had another drive, Will Griffin was probably going to go in. Those guys practice really hard.

At that point, I'm not saying, "Hey, we have to score again." If we score again, that's the nature of the deal. They were also bringing a lot of pressure. We had to get the ball on the perimeter and do some things because they were loading the box to stop the run late.

Those guys work incredibly hard all week. When their opportunities present themselves, we're going to let them play because we still have to develop those young players so they're more ready.

It was 1-0. That was the goal this week. We'll celebrate this a little bit tonight and then wake up tomorrow. We'll watch the tape, make corrections and then turn the page tomorrow night at about 5. Our staff meeting is at 4 tomorrow. As soon as that staff meeting is over, we'll watch special teams as a staff.

Then it's 1-0 and on to Campbell. It's about trying to win one game next week and focusing on that game all week. It's a good start. Being 1-0 was the goal this week, and we got there. Tomorrow at about 5, my mind will be 0-0 again.

It's just going into every game and focusing on one game at a time. It's coach speak, but that's how we operate.

Going back to it, we still need to figure out who we can rely on and who will be dependable. With the depth of our team, maybe on the line, there is still some room to figure that out. I wanted to see the backs go.

Rod Kearney came in. Caden (Jones) got in there, and Caden has started games before. He came in, and we need him to elevate his play. All those guys have to continue elevating. At offensive line, you have to get players ready to play because it's a long year.

You never know when their opportunity is going to come. You can't just think it doesn't matter whether he's getting better. We've got to get everybody in this program better. Everybody. Jadan Baugh has to get better. Everybody on our team has to continue getting better.

Those young linemen, Rod and Dice — Dice played some tackle that I liked. Those guys have to continue elevating so they can be dependable and reliable when their numbers are called.

Evan was available, but he had a little bit of a hip issue that wasn't feeling great. He didn't feel like he could do it. He was cleared to go but just didn't feel like he could push through it. I thought Duke did a really good job. London Montgomery is a good player back there, too. Byron Lewis did some good things tonight as well.
