title: Top DHS lawyer turns tables on 128 ex-judges after Bar declines ‘Worst of the Worst’ complaint
description: James Percival compared the 128 former judges' Florida Bar complaint to the Hunter Biden laptop controversy, calling the filing frivolous "Bar-fare."
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: DHS General Counsel James Percival is turning a complaint from 128 former judges back on its signers, calling on the Florida Bar to scrutinize those among them who are Bar members after it declined to investigate him.

The Bar said it does not investigate or prosecute sitting officers appointed under the U.S. Constitution while they are in office, a position Percival argued the complainants should have known before challenging his "Worst of the Worst Judges" series.

Percival accused the Florida Bar members who joined the complaint of potentially abusing the disciplinary process for political purposes, arguing their filing was frivolous and dubbing the tactic "Bar-fare."

"The 128 former judges are sort of an example of a tactic the left has used for a long time," Percival told Fox News Digital, comparing their appeal to professional authority to the 2020 controversy involving 51 former intelligence officials and Hunter Biden's laptop.

Dhs Eviscerates Media For 'Absolute Absurdity' Over Concern About 'Worst Of The Worst' Activist Judges List

Percival pointed to the Florida Bar's previous handling of a complaint involving former Attorney General Pam Bondi, arguing that they already signaled refusal to probe sitting presidential appointees.

"[W]hat these 128 former judges did was frivolous, and they were on notice that it was frivolous because the Florida Bar is very clear about this. So, it's 'Bar-fare'," he said, playing on the term "lawfare."

Liberal Law Professor Breaks With Obama Judge Over Trump Lawyer Crackdown: 'I Refuse To Teach' It

Percival said the same tactic has been used elsewhere, including the Hunter Biden laptop controversy and the way dissent over COVID-era restrictions was met with echoes of "trust the experts."

"The left has just like often hid behind this veneer, this prestige [of expertise] and they've gotten people who carry weight to carry their water for them. And I really think the emperor has no clothes on this, but we have to call it out and expose it."

When the political left does not want to publicly debate the merits of their assertion, they get figures who appear authoritative to shut down dissent, he said.

The comments came after rule-of-law groups Democracy Defenders Fund, Lawyers Defending American Democracy and 128 former federal and state judges filed a 24-page complaint accusing Percival of violating Florida's rules governing statements about judges. The complaint alleged that Percival, a licensed Florida attorney, violated ethics rules through "public attacks on sitting judges."

"His statements mischaracterized the judges' rulings and assailed their character and integrity. The ethics rules exist for a reason: Baseless attacks on judges by lawyers and public officials can undermine confidence in the courts and heighten the risk of physical threats against judges," Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement after the Bar declined to investigate the complaint.

Former Florida Supreme Court Chief Justice Peggy Quince, an appointee of Democratic ex-Gov. Lawton Chiles, led the judges' consortium.

The complaint focuses on four judges featured in Percival's "Worst of the Worst" posts, whom he accused of actions including "open defiance of the Supreme Court," "judicial sabotage" and "judicial micromanagement."

Supreme Court Weighs Trump Effort To Terminate Temporary Protections For Haitian, Syrian Migrants

The cases involved disputes over Temporary Protected Status, the government's handling of Kilmar Ábrego García and DHS use-of-force policies.

The complaint also referenced an article written by Percival condemning former President Joe Biden and a Rhode Island judge he appointed after an illegal immigrant whom DHS said had an international warrant for homicide was ordered released.

Percival said the activist judges themselves are the ones who are being a "disservice to the judiciary."

He argued that judges know their district court rulings can delay executive action when they cannot be immediately appealed.

As for the complainants, Percival said those who are themselves members of the Florida Bar should face scrutiny over whether they abused the complaint process for political purposes.

The Bar provided Fox News Digital a copy of its response sent to the Framingham, Massachusetts, address listed for the collective complainants.

Bar Counsel Christopher Wackes wrote his group does not investigate or prosecute "sitting officers appointed under the U.S. Constitution while they are in office." Wackes said any action could "encroach on the authority of the federal government."

He quipped situations like the bar complaint show he is over the proverbial target:

"[I]f people are this upset about what I'm doing, it must be having an effect that they don't like, which really just encourages me to keep going," he said, pressing conservatives to fight for their causes despite the knowledge the left will "try to ruin your life."

title: Florida State's defensive keys vs SMU
description: Florida State's defense will have one of their toughest tests this Saturday against SMU. Here are the keys for them on that side of the ball.
fullText:
It will be a spirited crowd on Monday night when the No. 19 SMU Mustangs come to Doak Campbell Stadium to take on the Florida State Seminoles. It's the ACC opener for both schools, and it will set the tone for conference play for each program in 2026.

FSU was able to pick up a win in their season opener thanks in large part to only allowing 17 points. With that said, they need to improve in multiple areas against SMU if they want to come out with a victory.

Here are five defensive keys for the Seminoles as they look to stop a very capable Mustangs offense.

It all starts in the trenches. This is a game where guys like Daniel Lyons, Deante McCray, Rylan Kennedy, and the Desir twins need to establish themselves from the get-go. If they can do that, they'll have a good chance of keeping SMU behind the chains.

Jennings is a dual-threat type of quarterback. So, Florida State's defense will need to keep him rattled while he's in the pocket, while also keeping a spy on him in case he tucks the ball and decides to run. This is an essential key for them.

Raphael is coming off a very productive season with the California Bears with over 900 rushing yards. FSU can't allow him to consistently move the chains because that will make them honest and open up the passing game. Stopping him is a crucial factor.

This is an area where Florida State struggled last week against the New Mexico State Aggies as they allowed 10 conversions on 17 attempts. It will be a tougher challenge against SMU, and they will make some plays on third down, but FSU can't let them convert at a high rate.

This ties into the previous point. Florida State can't let SMU's offense consistently drive past midfield and put themselves in a position to put up a lot of points. They have too many capable weapons on offense to allow that. Accomplishing this will give FSU's offense more opportunities to score, and the Seminoles will need all the points they can get in this one.

title: No celebrities, unpaid renewals, shuttered facilities: Medical pot in Florida faces severe headwinds
description: New proposed rules would ban the use of celebrities to endorse products are tougher than previous restrictions — and could increase worries about what comes next for a state where hopes were high for medical marijuana success.
fullText:
TALLAHASSEE, Florida — Gov. Ron DeSantis made his tough stance on medical marijuana a cornerstone of his conservative legacy in Florida. And as he prepares to leave office, the outlook for the more than $2 billion industry has investors and businesses alike fretting over the future.

With new state marketing restrictions, pot-growing facilities shutting down and firms unable to pay more than $1 million renewal fees on time, the state's once booming medical marijuana industry is in notable decline. There are currently 28 state-licensed medical pot companies operating 778 dispensaries across Florida.

Rules proposed by the state Office of Medical Marijuana late last month that would ban the use of celebrities to endorse products are tougher than previous restrictions — and could increase worries about what comes next for a state where hopes were high for medical marijuana success.

The buzzkill continues a DeSantis-era trend; the GOP governor increased licensing renewal fees by more than 2,000 percent before launching a campaign opposing a 2024 recreational legalization ballot initiative that ultimately failed to pass. The OMMU, which is responsible for crafting and implementing the state's rules around medical marijuana, now is pushing for further restrictions.

Joe Puglise, CEO of the newly licensed Fino Cannabis, said those would make attracting new patients almost impossible.

"How can we as a new company tell adults 21 and over that we're open for business and we're here to help patients?" Puglise said. "There's very little leeway today when you're a startup and you're bootstrapping yourself to do this and you don't have the three to four years to build out."

The proposed rules are the latest effort by DeSantis to cement his legacy as being tough on the medical marijuana industry. But it's not yet clear if the two candidates vying to replace him in November, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly, will bring any relief to the industry.

Already, Surterra, one of the first companies to receive a state license to sell and grow medical marijuana almost 10 years ago, recently announced the closure of two major growing facilities in Florida and laid off more than 100 workers. Surterra is owned by the Atlanta-based Parallel. Parallel did not respond to an email with questions about the recent Surterra layoffs.

Jake Bergmann, who founded Surterra but is no longer involved in the state's pot industry, was critical of the direction Florida took on marijuana, which is now legal for medical use in 41 states in the U.S. and Washington.

title: Woman who fatally shot man during confrontation over parking space won't be charged
description: Prosecutors found she had a right to stand her ground, under Florida law.
fullText:
A Florida woman who fatally shot a man in the parking lot of a Walmart during a confrontation over a parking space won't face charges, prosecutors announced Thursday.

The Broward County State Attorney's Office said Florida's "stand your ground" law makes the shooter, who said she was acting in self-defense, immune from prosecution in connection with the June 30 shooting in North Lauderdale.

Bart Diguglielmo, 62, was shot and killed in the incident, which was captured on several videos, including from cellphones and a Tesla, according to a memo on the shooting released Thursday by the Broward County State Attorney's Office.

Man fatally shot in Walmart parking lot following dispute over parking space: Authorities

"A dispute over a parking space. In a Walmart parking lot. The facts surrounding the June 30, 2026, homicide of Bart DiGuglielmo are as tragic as they are absurd," Broward State Attorney's Office Homicide Trial Unit Division Chief Stephen Zaccor wrote in the memo. "There is relatively no dispute about what actually happened because the entire incident was captured by various video recording devices."

The shooter, identified in the memo as Melissa Payne, was driving with her niece and niece's baby when she and Diguglielmo got into a "brief stalemate" after attempting to park in the same spot, the memo said.

DiGuglielmo "inexplicably abandoned his car in the through lane of travel" and went into the store, before shortly returning to his vehicle, according to the memo. Multiple witnesses reported hearing him say he was going to "mess her car up" and "---- her s--- up," before driving off at a high rate of speed, parking and then walking toward Payne's vehicle, according to the memo. A witness described him as being "visibly angry" while looking at Payne, according to the memo.

Payne exited her vehicle holding a phone in her left hand and a firearm in her right and said, per a witness, "If you keep coming up to me, I'm going to ------- shoot you!" the memo stated.

The witness reported that "despite those warnings," DiGuglielmo continued to approach, and video showed him "aggressively approach" Payne, according to the memo.

DiGuglielmo "continued his pursuit" as Payne backed away from him, according to the memo. He is seen on video continuing to pursue her and "motioned as if he was going to damage" her vehicle with his keys, according to the memo.

DiGuglielmo turned back and then approached Payne, at which point she fired her gun, striking him in the abdomen, according to the memo.

Payne was on the phone with her husband during the shooting, who told authorities that she said, "Bae, I shot. Call the cops," according to the memo.

She was briefly taken into custody by the Broward Sheriff's Office and her "recitation of the facts was consistent with the various sources of video evidence," the memo stated. She was released after stating she acted in self-defense, prosecutors said.

2 killed, multiple hurt in shooting at Minneapolis apartment building: Police

In an analysis of the incident, Zaccor stated that Payne was "in a public place, a Walmart parking lot, and therefore was in a place she had a right to be." She further is not a convicted felon and had a right to possess a firearm, "therefore she was not doing anything unlawful at the time she used deadly force," he wrote.

"Accordingly," Zaccor continued, Payne "had the right to stand her ground if she was in reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm." Based on the evidence, the state is unable to prove that her fear of great bodily harm was "not reasonable," he wrote, citing DiGuglielmo's actions.

Zaccor said that because Florida is a stand-your-ground state, Payne "did not have to wait to be attacked before resorting to deadly force. She did not have to retreat as long as her fear was reasonable and no evidence has been presented to disprove that."

The new skipper was brief in his opening statement. "Our team, we had practice this morning," he noted. "We play Saturday at 7:55 against FAU and we're excited about it."

Sumrall went on to discuss topics such as his SEC head coaching debut, the quarterback room, offensive line coach Phil Trautwein, JACK Jayden Woods, the special teams and more.

Take a look below at everything Sumrall had to offer at the Week 1 SEC teleconference.

You gotta play with enthusiasm and passion, effort, and you wanna see them strain. You only get 12 regular season opportunities and you don't want to take any of them for granted, ever. And I'd like for us to play like we've practiced, you know? Look like we've done some things before and operate efficiently.

You see so many common mistakes that happen in Week 1 or Week 0 games like last week, and just for us to do what we've prepared in a crisp, clean manner is sort of the way you want to see it happen. But there will be guys making mistakes; when they do, I want to see them make them full speed. I want to see them go as hard as they can from the snap through the echo of the whistle.

Phil is really detailed. He's a great teacher. He's very consistent. Phil's a guy who doesn't get too high or too low, he shows up the same way every day. Like I said, consistency is a key there, I think. And I think just finding ways to help guys maximize who they are. Different guys receive things in different ways from a coaching standpoint, and so, how we reach each player is a little bit unique.

But he's very thorough with his preparation for his guys and I think he's done a great job. I did not shy away from — when we got here, I felt that the offensive line was an area that needed massive improvement. I think we've made improvements. Is it high enough for us to play the game at a level that we desire to? We're gonna find out real soon.

I'm gonna be pretty excited about it. I've said this a lot: I think back to when I was on the opposite sideline a couple times here as a player and as a coach, and how unique and special I've always felt like the Swamp is. And the fanbase here is so electric and charged up that I'll be very similarly wired. That gameday opportunity here is unlike many out there. And so, I'll be amped up.

But at the end of the day too, it's really about focusing on us doing our job to the best of our ability and playing really good football. And so, you have to make sure that while you're emotionally charged up and you're hyped, that you don't forget that the main things that go on within the game aren't in the stands; it's in between the white lines, and how do we help put our guys in situations to be successful.

I appreciate the shout-out to Ronny Massey. What a great man. You know, I feel appreciation every day I walk into our building. We've got the Gator head logo above our main entrance, and every time I walk in our building, I get excited about being here. And I don't take any day at the office for granted.

But, you know, to your point, growing up, I really idolized SEC football. I would watch every SEC game that was on TV or listen to a bunch of them on the radio as a kid, and to be able to have the privilege of leading an SEC team as a head coach is something I've dreamed about my entire coaching career. And, for me, it's the opportunity of a lifetime, and I will never take it for granted and will always have great appreciation for the situation I'm in.

I'd say, if you asked me early April who was going to start for us, really wasn't much of a conversation, just because of the difference of how well Philo operated at the line of scrimmage and ran the offense. The beautiful thing is Philo's continued to grow and get better, but so has the room. Tramell has stepped up and made strides. Aidan Warner has been really consistent and steady when he's had opportunities present. Will Griffin is uber talented, the freshman we got from Tampa. And then, Aaron Williams is also in that room, does a great job adding value to our football team.

But the whole room is elevated, which has made it more competitive, which is good for everybody. You know, you don't want anybody to become the starter because there's not great depth in the room. You want one guy just to elevate a little bit above the others, and I've got a lot of confidence in everybody in that quarterback room, though, that when they have opportunities, they're going to be ready to go.

I think it is, but you never know until you play. I think in preparation our urgency has improved. I think what you find out on Saturday is what your level of detail and doing your job at an elite level against another team, and it's not maybe in a practice environment against maybe people you play against every day. There's going to be some adversity hit in every game at every point all year. That's the biggest thing you can't really fully prepare for.

We simulate a lot of things to try and create what that looks like around our building and practices all the time. But there's nothing like it happening in a live game. We'll see what our urgency looks like against another opponent here shortly. I look forward to seeing how we respond to a lot of different situations that come up within games.

We've got Patrick Durkin as our starting field goal kicker. He was 25 of 28 last year and had a handful of them, I think four over 50 yards. So he's steady. He's got real ability. Yesterday on kickoffs, he was hitting most of them, eight, nine deep in the end zone, so he's got high touchback capability.

Alec Clark is our punter who's been starting punter in college football now for a couple of years. He's really efficient, catch-to-kick. He's usually fast getting the ball off and really is a consistent punter in regards to distance and hang. I like how he does things. The other thing that Alec does at an elite level is he handles the short snaps really well on field goal and extra points. He's as good of a holder as I've ever been around, which probably doesn't get talked about enough.

Snapping-wise, Carter Milliron will handle our long snaps on punt. He's played a lot of college football as a fifth-year senior. Then Lincoln Anderson is going to handle our short snaps, who is a true freshman from Hoover, Alabama, but has done a really good job this entire training camp and really shown that he is ready for this moment. Look forward to watching him perform, so those are our main specialists that will start and go on Saturday.

My first impression was positive, and it's only become more positive after that. He's a guy; when we got here, he was a high priority for us to retain. Then he made the decision to enter the transfer portal to just test the waters and see what was out there. We were able to hold on and get him to stay at the University of Florida, and I was pretty excited when that happened.

I'm even more excited about the fact that he made the decision to stay each and every day that I get to work with him. He's really, really talented. But more so than just being talented, he's as good of a human you could ever want to be around. He works at a really high level. He's very detailed. He's got great pride in his craft, and he's a high-character guy. I think the sky is the limit for what Jayden can achieve on the field.

But what makes it fun working with him day in, day out is just — holistically, he's a fantastic person. He has high standards for himself in every area of his life and not just football. He's going to be successful in any endeavor he takes on just because of the way he's wired. So very grateful he's on our football team. Like I said, I was excited off my first impression that we got to keep him. I'm even more excited now.

title: FSU football running game may be best chance at pulling off SMU upset
description: Florida State football's first stock market is open: Three Seminoles are surging, three are slipping after the 34-17 win over New Mexico State.
fullText:
Florida State opened the 2026 season with a 34-17 victory over New Mexico State, but one game provided plenty of insight into which players are trending upward and which still have questions to answer.

While it's far too early for overreactions, the Seminoles' season opener offered an early glimpse of who's building momentum heading into Monday night's ACC showdown against SMU. From standout performances in the backfield to concerns along both lines of scrimmage, here's Florida State's first stock report of the season.

Kromah looked every bit like the feature that Florida State envisioned entering the season.

The sophomore consistently wore down New Mexico State's defense while displaying the explosiveness and elusiveness that made him one of the Seminoles' most anticipated players. He finished with 115 rushing yards on 14 carries, highlighted by a 52-yard run that helped set the tone offensively.

With high expectations surrounding him as FSU's lead back, Kromah delivered an encouraging start to the season.

Few players impacted the game in more ways than Singleton.

The versatile playmaker contributed as a runner, receiver and return specialist, totaling 164 all-purpose yards and two touchdowns. His performance earned him ACC Receiver of the Week honors on Monday.

"Sam's a guy who's a really talented football player," head coach Mike Norvell said. "He's growing, just in all areas. I was proud of him to see his impact in all three phases of it."

Singleton and Kromah already appear capable of forming one of the conference's most dynamic backfield tandems. If that continues, it should take pressure off quarterback Ashton Daniels and create more balance in Florida State's offense.

Jones' return to full strength could be one of Florida State's biggest developments on defense.

The cornerback, who spent much of the offseason working back from a season-ending injury, looked confident in coverage. He recorded a pass breakup and an interception while making several plays on deep-ball attempts.

"You've seen him grow mentally off the field, on the field now," Norvell said.

"He gets to start tonight. He has a PBU, gets the interception in the end zone. Take us through the growth from him, his mentality, and what you're going to expect from him this season."

Defensive coordinator Tony White praised Jones on Monday, noting he was among the defense's top performers in the opener. His emergence adds another playmaker to an already talented secondary.

"He's been acting right like he's the best version of himself on and off the field, and it's translated," White said.

There were understandable questions about Gbayor after an injury sidelined him throughout spring practice.

The veteran linebacker quickly eased those concerns against New Mexico State. Playing in a rotational role, Gbayor recorded four tackles and a sack while bringing physicality and energy to Florida State's defense.

His familiarity with White's 3-3-5 system, dating back to their time together at Nebraska, continues to make him a valuable piece of one of the Seminoles' deepest position groups.

Danzy's transition from running back to wide receiver appears to be taking another significant step forward.

The Tallahassee native tied Singleton for the team lead with four receptions and finished with 51 receiving yards. His best play came on a skinny post route in the first quarter that helped set up a scoring opportunity.

With Duce Robinson expected to draw considerable attention from opposing defenses, Danzy has a chance to emerge as a reliable secondary receiving option.

Florida State's offensive line remains a work in progress, but Pabst was one of its brightest spots in the opener.

The Bowling Green transfer started at right guard and even saw snaps as an extra tight end. According to Pro Football Focus, Pabst did not allow a sack or pressure across 69 snaps.

Offensive line coach Herb Hand called Pabst the unit's most consistent player before the season, and the former All-MAC lineman backed up that praise in Week 0.

After promising freshman seasons, Mandrell and Darryll Desir had relatively quiet starts to their sophomore campaigns.

Mandrell finished with four tackles, while Darryll was credited with one. More concerning was the lack of consistent pressure generated by either player as Florida State searched for disruption along the defensive front.

The Seminoles will need more production from both linemen against an SMU offense expected to present a tougher challenge.

Wisner's stock dips more because of usage than performance.

The former Texas running back was expected to be part of a three-man rotation alongside Kromah and Singleton, but he saw the fewest opportunities among the group's primary contributors. Wisner totaled 34 yards on four carries, averaging an impressive 8.5 yards per attempt.

His limited workload was one of the more surprising developments of the opener. The good news for Wisner is that one game doesn't define a season, and his role could expand as conference play begins.

Nwaiwu endured a difficult debut at right tackle.

According to Pro Football Focus, the Stephen F. Austin transfer was responsible for five pressures, the most on the team. He surrendered one sack, one quarterback hit and three hurries as New Mexico State found success attacking his side of the line.

There's still plenty of time for improvement, particularly as Nwaiwu adjusts to a higher level of competition, but his performance will be one of the areas Florida State must address before facing SMU.

title: Woods gets five-year driving ban after plea agreement over car crash
description: Tiger Woods has been banned from driving for five years and hit with a fine after entering a plea agreement for reckless driving following a car crash in Florida in March. The 15-time major winner was arrested and spent eight hours in jail before being bailed after his Land Rover rolled over in a collision with a pick-up truck towing a trailer.
fullText:
Tiger Woods has been banned from driving for five years and hit with a fine after entering a plea agreement for reckless driving following a car crash in Florida in March.

The 15-time major winner was arrested and spent eight hours in jail before being bailed after his Land Rover rolled over in a collision with a pick-up truck towing a trailer.

He had previously entered a written plea of not guilty via his lawyers to charges of driving under the influence, property damage and a refusal to submit to testing.

Appearing at Martin County Courthouse on Wednesday morning, he agreed to the lesser charge, with Judge Darren Steele ordering Woods' driving licence be suspended for five years alongside a fine of $1,000. An additional careless driving citation also carries a five-year suspension, but the judge allowed that to run concurrently.

Woods walked away unhurt from the crash, escaping out of his passenger door, and, while he passed a breathalyser test for alcohol, the 50-year-old refused to submit to a urinary test for drugs. That refusal earned him an additional $500.

According to the initial police affidavit, Woods was observed by the investigating officers to be "sweating profusely" while acting "lethargic and slow" with eyes that were "bloodshot and glassy".

He admitted he "was looking down at his cell phone and changing the radio station" in the moments before the crash and "did not notice the vehicle in front of him had slowed down".

Woods told the authorities he had not consumed any alcohol but admitted to taking "a few" prescription medications and had done so earlier in the morning while insisting he had not had any illegal drugs.

Multiple sobriety exercises were conducted, where he struggled to follow instructions, leading a deputy to conclude: "How he performed on the exercises and based on my training, knowledge and experience, I believe Woods' normal faculties were impaired and he was unable to safely operate the motor vehicle."

Woods underwent emergency surgery after suffering multiple leg injuries following a serious car accident in California in February 2021. He has not competed on the PGA Tour since July 2024.

The affidavit stated Woods said he had 20 surgeries on his leg as a result of that crash, plus seven operations on his back, while the report also noted Woods was "limping and stumbling."

Woods later wrote on X: "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in.

"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritize my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."

Woods was also arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence (DUI) offences in 2017 after being found asleep at the wheel of his car in Jupiter, Florida.

He later pleaded guilty to reckless driving after it emerged he had had five prescription drugs in his system at the time.

In 2009, he crashed his car into a fire hydrant and tree outside his home in an incident that led to a spectacular unravelling of his private life.

title: He killed his 16-year-old ex-girlfriend 50 years ago. Florida just executed him.
description: The state executed Harold Gene Lucas by lethal injection for the 1976 murder of 16-year-old Jill Piper. Lucas was 24 at the time of the crime and was on death row for 50 years.
fullText:
Florida has executed a 74-year-old inmate who spent five decades on death row for shooting his teenage ex-girlfriend seven times even as she begged for her life. It's the first of eight scheduled executions in the U.S. in September, the most in a single month since 2010.

The state executed Harold Gene Lucas by lethal injection on Tuesday, Sept. 1, for the 1976 murder of 16-year-old Jill Piper in Bonita Springs, halfway between Fort Myers and Naples on Florida's Gulf Coast. Lucas was 24 at the time of murder.

Lucas, who was pronounced dead at 6:18 p.m. ET, became the 14th inmate executed in Florida this year, by far the most of any state. Florida governor Ron DeSantis continues an aggressive death penalty push as the end of his term approaches.

Lucas chose to accept his execution and waive further appeals after DeSantis signed his death warrant in July.

"I am 75 years old," Lucas recently told a court, though his 75th birthday would have been on Halloween. "I've been on death row for 50 years, and I have no desire to carry this any further . . . The sooner it's over, the better I'll enjoy it. I am tired."

Jill's brother, Buck Piper, told the Gulf Coast News that his father died waiting for justice but said that his 86-year-old mother would be front and center among the witnesses to the execution.

"They never got over the loss of their daughter," he told the station. "It's something that still weighs on her mind to this day."

Here's what you need to know about the execution, the crime, and why September is setting up to be the busiest single month for executions in 16 years.

On Aug. 14, 1976, Lucas had been drinking and doing hard drugs, got in a fight at a gas station, and told his friends he was going to "put that little (expletive) in a hole," according to court documents.

As Jill was returning home from a dance around midnight with two friends − 17-year-old Terri Rice and 19-year-old Richard Byrd Jr. − Lucas was lying in wait. Lucas fired four gunshots into Piper's back, and Rice and Byrd ran inside to call for help, court records say.

Though bleeding from the gunshot wounds, Piper was able to run inside. But Lucas followed, took her back outside and shot her three more times, including once in the back of the head, after she pleaded for her life. He then shot Byrd in the stomach and Rice in the hip. Both of them survived.

Lucas and Jill had dated for about four years when she broke up with him after an argument.

Part of the reason it has taken Florida so long to execute Lucas is because his death sentenced was vacated several times over the years, largely over procedural errors. Lucas has been re-sentenced to death altogether four times over the decades.

"It was an execution, pure and simple," prosecutor John Dommerich argued to jurors just before Lucas was sentenced to death for a fourth time in 1987, according to an archived story in the Naples Daily News, part of the USA TODAY Network. "He executed her when she begged for her life."

Lucas' attorneys had argued that he deserved mercy, saying he would never have killed Jill if he hadn't been drunk and high on hard drugs that night, including PCP.

At 16, Jill Piper was just getting started in life and was known for being just as sweet as she could be spunky, her younger brother, David Piper Jr., told the Naples Daily News on the 30th anniversary of her murder in 2006.

"She was tough," David Piper said at the time. "It was a scrappy little town here for many, many years, and she could take most of the guys, no problem ... But you can't fight bullets."

Even at 13, David Piper said he knew that Lucas was bad news and warned his sister to stay away from him. But, he said, Jill saw the good in everybody.

"She cared about people to the extreme," he said. "That's why she didn't get to live a long, fruitful life. Sometimes when people care to the extreme, they leave themselves wide open for dangerous situations to occur."

He told the newspaper that he tried not to think too much about his sister and didn't keep photos of her around.

"The only thing that will help is when Gene Lucas is put to death," he said.

Eight executions are scheduled to be carried out in five states this month. The executions include that of Christa Pike, the first woman set to be put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

The last time at least eight executions were carried out in a single month in the U.S. was in 2010, according to a USA TODAY analysis of data tracked by the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center. That year, five states carried out nine executions in the month of May.

This month's spate of executions comes amid an overall uptick in the death penalty in the U.S. in the last two years. In 2025, 11 states executed 47 inmates, the most in any single year since 2009. So far this year, 24 inmates have been executed, with another 13 on the calendar through December, though more are expected to be added.

Experts attribute the increases to a friendlier death penalty climate under President Donald Trump and Florida's particularly aggressive execution push in the last two years.

Of the 71 executions carried out in the U.S. since 2025, Florida accounts for 32 of them. That's 45%, and that figure is increasing. Of this year's 24 executions, Florida has carried out 14. That's 58%.

Gov. Ron DeSantis, who decides which inmates are executed and when, has been drawing increasing criticism from death penalty opponents and observers who say the governor is being motivated by political ambition ahead of the 2028 presidential election and is "increasingly treating executions as routine instruments of political power," according to a recent statement from Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.

DeSantis, whose second term as governor ends in January, has said he wants to give closure to families who have waited for justice sometimes longer than four decades.

Amanda Lee Myers is a senior crime reporter who covers cold case investigations and the death penalty for USA TODAY. Follow her on X at @amandaleeusat.

fullText:
The 2026 Florida State Seminoles are in an intriguing position. After a pair of seasons missing the College Football Playoff, they are looking to get back to the success they had a few years ago. With a Week 0 win already in their pocket as they attempt to get back into a bowl game, there are some people who are not believing in them this season. Let's take a closer look at one college football analyst who isn't buying the Seminoles this season.

While on Josh Pate's College Football Show, Pate made it known that he did not like what he saw from the Florida State Seminoles in their 34-17 Week 0 victory over New Mexico State.

"If you watched the game like I did, what was most alarming is just how evenly matched the teams looked for a lot of the night. The better team won here. Florida State is a superior team. I thought it would be end first quarter, 21-0. Go to half, 42-3. I expected that because there won't be a lot of those opportunities this year for Florida State. So I expected it, and it didn't happen, and I don't think because somebody was overlooking someone. I just don't think Florida State's team is that good."

The schedule will get tougher than playing New Mexico State. Pate explained how the schedule is not favorable for Florida State this year.

"Playing SMU and then in Tuscaloosa and then home for Virginia and then at Louisville, at Miami, and Clemson by Halloween is a recipe for disaster."

After a pair of bad seasons with a combined record of 7-17, Seminoles coach Mike Norvell cannot afford to be out of the College Football Playoff picture that early into the season. Even with a tough schedule, the Seminoles are hoping to make some noise in the ACC and get into the 12-team playoff. It will be intriguing to see how this program looks, as they were able to get some rust off against an inferior opponent.

title: Byron Donalds shuts down Bill Maher’s claim on GOP primary racism, says 'Florida is a meritocracy'
description: Byron Donalds pushed back on Bill Maher's claims that racism cost him key Florida Panhandle counties, calling the state a meritocracy on "Real Time."
fullText:
Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds rejected comedian Bill Maher's claims that Donalds lost key counties in the recent primary in part due to the racism within the state.

Appearing on HBO's "Real Time with Bill Maher" Friday night, Donalds, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, pushed back on Maher's assertion that he lost parts of Florida's Panhandle because of the area's predominantly White electorate.

"You did lose the 'Redneck Riviera' badly," Maher said, referring to Donalds' losses in Calhoun, Columbia, Dixie, Gilchrist, Hamilton, Hardee, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Levy, Liberty, Madison, Suwannee, Taylor, Union and Washington counties, rural counties where roughly 94% of Republican voters are White.

Stephen A Smith Admits Byron Donalds Could Make Him A Republican, Calls Him 'The Real Deal'

"I can't get with you on a lot of this policy stuff," Maher continued. "But I think it would be great if the country did have [its] first Black, Republican governor."

Maher went on to praise Donalds for his willingness to run in "this post-racial world" where constituents don't care about the "color of their skin," but he added that "we're not quite there yet though."

Bill Maher Blasts California's Education Results, Cites Two Surging Red States

"The Redneck Riviera, which is the Panhandle," Maher began. "I think there are people there who still would not — you're a Republican, you're a Trumper — they should love you and they don't. I think there is still racism.

"Let's talk a little bit about the Panhandle," Donalds replied, beginning his rebuttal. "There are counties we did incredibly well in that we won. There were some counties that we fell a little short in, that's OK."

Watch: Byron Donalds Brushes Off Gop Debate Demands As Rivals Lag Far Behind In Polls

Donalds then pointed out the crowded Florida primary field which had 11 Republicans on the ballot, with candidates "who had various lines of support."

"The No. 1 thing overall, we closed out 48% of the vote in Florida," Donalds said. "Eight hundred thousand votes [is] a long way to becoming the nominee."

Trump-backed Nominees Dominate Primary Contests As President Tightens Party Vice Grip

Donalds went on to push back against Maher's argument that racial bias influenced the primary results, insisting that Florida is a place where people can pursue opportunities in elected office.

"Florida really has become the microcosm of what we all want," Donalds said. "It's a meritocracy. And it's about the best person with the best views, the best skills, the best talent moving forward to represent your state or to represent a district in your state, and Florida exemplifies that."

Gianno Caldwell: Florida Needs Byron Donalds To Protect The Desantis Legacy

However, former Florida state Sen. Dave Aronberg was not as quick to attribute Donalds' showing to the crowded primary field.

"When you look at the primary numbers, Byron Donalds falling short of 50% does raise some legitimate questions," Aronberg told Fox News Digital.

"Yes, there were 11 names on the ballot, but few of his opponents were viable contenders, and Donalds had a massive fundraising and name recognition advantage compared to the rest of the field. It wasn't exactly a neck-and-neck dogfight.

Fox News Power Rankings: Democrats Lead In The House, But Redistricting Keeps The Gop In The Game

"When you see him underperforming in certain rural pockets, it's hard to completely dismiss race having played at least some quiet role. Going into November, Republicans have a massive advantage in party registration and financial resources.

"But this will be no cakewalk based on what we saw in the primary, along with President Trump's lagging poll numbers and the quality of his Democratic opponent."

'Captain Canada' Firebrand Unloads On Trump With Profane One-liner As Trade War Escalates

Maher later challenged Donalds on his campaign platform by pointing to President Donald Trump's tariffs impacting affordability across the country — especially in Florida.

"I don't feel like the president's policies are making that affordable part easy for you," Maher said.

A Popular Cocktail Has A Trump Trade Problem You Probably Didn't Know About

"Even the Wall Street Journal, which is usually pretty far right, calls this trade war with Canada the 'dumbest trade war,' that's the title," Maher continued. "It says Republicans are already getting pounded on the campaign trail over his tariffs and inflation, mostly because of the war. Byron, are you getting pounded on the campaign trail?"

"I think that people in Florida are thinking about their pocketbooks. Well, that's like anywhere else," Donalds said.

Donalds defended Trump's tariffs on Canada, adding that the president is reevaluating trade policies that are not working for the American people.

"But I would rather have a chief executive that looks at these deals and engages these other countries and fights for Americans, [rather] than just let them roll knowing that they're not gonna be in the interest of small businesses," Donalds said.

title: Olympic Sprinter Marvin Bracy-Williams Arrested on DUI Charge Months After 12-Year USADA Ban
description: Former Olympic sprinter Marvin Bracy-Williams was arrested on a DUI charge in Orlando, Florida, on Aug. 3, adding a new legal issue to a year ... Read More
fullText:
Former Olympic sprinter Marvin Bracy-Williams was arrested on a DUI charge in Orlando, Florida, on Aug. 3, adding a new legal issue to a year already marked by a lengthy anti-doping sanction and his notice of retirement.

According to court documents obtained by TMZ Sports, the arrest followed a roadside encounter after Bracy-Williams' vehicle ended up in a ditch and a tow truck driver requested law enforcement at the scene.

TMZ reported the arrest on Aug. 28. The outlet's report did not identify a blood-alcohol result or a final disposition in the case, and an arrest does not establish guilt.

The case surfaced less than three months after the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency imposed a 12-year period of ineligibility on Bracy-Williams for his third anti-doping rule violation. He notified USADA of his intent to retire on the same day that sanction was announced.

The tow truck driver told officers that he came upon Bracy-Williams' vehicle and found the athlete apparently passed out in the driver's seat while the engine was running and the vehicle was still in gear, according to TMZ's account of the court documents. By the time police arrived, the tow truck was pulling the vehicle from the ditch.

The driver told police that he contacted his employer and requested law enforcement because he believed Bracy-Williams was intoxicated. An officer reported smelling alcohol and said Bracy-Williams performed poorly during field sobriety testing before he was taken into custody on the DUI charge.

Bracy-Williams was already serving a 45-month anti-doping sanction when USADA announced another 12-year period of ineligibility on June 5. The latest violation stemmed from three whereabouts failures recorded on July 1, 2025, Feb. 24, 2026, and April 1, 2026.

Three whereabouts failures within a 12-month period constitute an anti-doping rule violation. USADA said a first whereabouts violation ordinarily carries a one- to two-year period of ineligibility, but because this was Bracy-Williams' third anti-doping rule violation, he faced an increased range of eight years to a lifetime ban. The agency determined that 12 years was appropriate under the circumstances.

His earlier 45-month sanction was announced in November 2025 after a USADA investigation involving testosterone use, attempted tampering and a separate whereabouts violation. USADA said Bracy-Williams admitted his violations and provided substantial assistance, resulting in significant reductions to part of the sanction he otherwise faced. A 24-month penalty for the earlier whereabouts violation was then added to the reduced 21-month sanction for the testosterone and tampering violations, bringing the total to 45 months.

The newer 12-year sanction is required to run consecutively after his previous period of ineligibility. Because Bracy-Williams notified USADA of his intent to retire on June 5, the agency said his remaining period of ineligibility will continue indefinitely until he returns from retirement and serves the remainder of his sanctions.

Bracy-Williams returned to competition outside the traditional World Athletics system shortly before the latest sanction. Enhanced announced in January that he would join its sprint field while he was still serving his previous USADA suspension, and he went on to finish third in the men's 100 meters at the inaugural Enhanced Games in Las Vegas in May, a result also noted by the New York Post.

The Enhanced Games permits athletes to use performance-enhancing substances that are prohibited in traditional sanctioned competition under its own competition framework. The event has positioned that policy as a defining difference from organizations operating under the World Anti-Doping Code.

USADA's June ruling also disqualified Bracy-Williams from competitive results on and after April 1, 2026, with the agency stating that applicable medals, points and prizes are subject to forfeiture.

Four years before the latest legal and anti-doping developments, Bracy-Williams entered the 2022 World Athletics Championships in Eugene as one of the leading American sprinters. He won his opening 100-meter heat in 10.05 seconds and advanced through the rounds to the final.

Bracy-Williams crossed the line in 9.88 seconds in the final, taking silver behind Fred Kerley's 9.86 as the United States swept all three medals. Trayvon Bromell also ran 9.88 and took bronze.

Bracy-Williams earned another silver as part of the U.S. men's 4x100-meter relay team at those championships. He had previously represented the United States at the 2016 Rio Olympics, advancing to the 100-meter semifinals.

title: Florida native Ross Chastain calls Daytona Cup pole a "life achievement"
description: Chastain grew up less than two hours away from Daytona International Speedway
fullText:
Ross Chastain has never been known for his qualifying performances. In fact, he became the only driver to ever win the Coca-Cola 600 from last place on the grid in 2025.

But Friday at Daytona, he rocketed to the top of the charts, taking pole position by half-a-tenth over Chris Buescher.

It's just Chastain's third career pole in the NASCAR Cup Series, with his other two P1s coming at Watkins Glen in 2024 and Nashville in 2023 (a race he won).

"Yeah, it's almost indescribable," Chastain said of the pole in a post-qualifying press conference. "I think I should probably start with, like, I grasp that it doesn't have much bearing on knowing what tomorrow is going to bring, but for tonight and today for a new package, for Trackhouse to go and pick the right things for car build to come here and to execute through two rounds, it's incredible. We've been good in one round before, but not the second. So, yeah, it's very important to note that we chose the right things as a team to come here and execute through qualifying.

"I'll start this with -- I do not know what that means for tomorrow. I'm being honest, I have no idea what it means for tomorrow."

Of course, as Chastain notes, qualifying means very little a superspeedway. Last year, Ryan Blaney won the race from P1, but qualifying was rained out. The last true Daytona pole-sitter to win the race was Dale Earnhardt Jr. in the summer of 2015.

But besides that, it's still a very special moment for the Florida driver.

"Life achievement," said Chastain. "I was a kid sitting in the grandstands. We camped outside of turn one, gate 40. For those that remember back in, I don't know, late 90s, 2000s, early 2000s, it was not the nice, beautiful gate 40 with dry grass that you see now. It was a mud pit. We camped over there, rode our bikes around and had other families that were family and some that were more than family that were such close friends and my buddies that I grew up with.

"So, yeah, I mean, from the race pools, like getting the race day paper and drawing names out that they would cut up and hoping you got the pole-sitter, that was a big deal. And as I got older, I realized how much little or just less it means, as far as how the car is going to draft. But, still, it's a big deal. It's a life achievement that I will never forget. This is a moment I'll never forget."

It was also a great day for Trackhouse as an organization, with Chastain's teammates Shane van Gisbergen and Connor Zilisch qualifying sixth and seventh, respectively.

SVG is trying to hold onto the 16th and final spot inside the Chase field, and Chastain is fully aware of the role he may play in that battle.

"When there's an opportunity of two cars in front of me, I think everybody in the field knows that I'll push the 97 [SVG]," said Chastain. "I am OEM loyal and specifically 97 loyal. So when there's opportunity, any momentum I have, any push I have, will go to the 97. The crew chiefs will be talking. You know, there's little differences, and if we find something air pressure wise or something, the 97 will be the first to know."

However, Chastain surely wants to win too, as he is facing a winless streak that dates back to Memorial Day Weekend, 2025. Daytona will mark 49 races since his last trip to Cup Series Victory Lane, and the driver of the No. 1 has also managed to win at least one race in every year of the Next Gen era (since 2022).

title: Florida grand jury finds DeSantis administration misused $10 million, but no charges filed
description: A Florida grand jury found that Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' administration “misappropriated” $10 million in taxpayer money it diverted to a charity connected to his wife, but it declined to file cri...
fullText:
A Florida grand jury found that Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' administration "misappropriated" $10 million in taxpayer money it diverted to a charity connected to his wife, but it declined to file criminal charges due to a lack of evidence indicating who specifically was responsible.

DeSantis on Thursday did not dispute the legitimacy of the secret grand jury report obtained and published online by CBS News Miami, but he insisted no laws were broken and said whoever leaked the sealed documents would face "consequences."

The Leon County grand jury completed its report in January on investigations into Hope Florida, the charity started in 2021 by Florida first lady Casey DeSantis. Despite the lack of charges, the report ignited a new round of criticism aimed at DeSantis and other top state Republicans over the charity receiving $10 million from a state Medicaid settlement intended to help poor children get health insurance.

David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor, called for the grand jury probe to be reopened. He faces Republican Byron Donalds in November. DeSantis, under Florida law, cannot seek a third term.

The Hope Florida charity is supposed to help financially struggling families connect with churches and aid groups to help keep them off publicly-financed assistance programs. The $10 million was instead moved to political action committees that used the money to oppose a 2024 statewide ballot measure that would have legalized marijuana for adults in the state.

DeSantis opposed the measure, and it fell just short of the 60% supermajority it needed to become law.

"Despite our finding that the money was misappropriated, we find insufficient evidence to charge anyone criminally," the report concluded.

The grand jury said no one would take responsibility for sending the money to the charity or had any memory of who did.

"We recognize that this would be an impediment to criminal prosecution," the report noted. "While we can't prove who is responsible, we can plainly see that taxpayer money was misused for political purposes and we would like to see changes made to prevent this from happening again."

The grand jury report concluded that James Uthmeier, who was DeSantis' chief of staff at the time, "was in a position of authority over those involved in settling," and that his Keep Florida Clean PAC was the prime recipient of the $10 million. The grand jury said then-state Attorney General Ashley Moody's office knew of the plans to divert the money. She was later appointed by DeSantis to the U.S. Senate.

Uthmeier and Moody are both seeking reelection.

In a news conference Thursday, Uthmeier suggested Democrats were behind the grand jury report leak and called renewed interest in its findings "a politically motivated hoax."

In a post on X on Thursday, Moody said her office was only one of several agencies that signed off on the initial settlement, and "had no knowledge of how funds would be spent" by Hope Florida, state lawmakers or any other group.

title: Florida Students Punished for Silent Protest Against ICE Get Free Speech Victory in Federal Court
description: A federal judge sided with the Florida International University students who sued over their school's student expression policy.
fullText:
A group of Florida students returning to college may have scored a temporary free speech win, but their legal battle may not be over.

On Sunday, a federal judge ruled that Florida International University (FIU) likely violated students' free speech rights when the school punished students for silently protesting indoors, reported Axios. In her ruling, U.S. Southern District of Florida Judge Jacqueline Becerra issued a preliminary injunction, preventing the school from enforcing its expressive activity rule against the students.

The case stems from an incident in March when a group of students wearing shirts saying "ICE OFF FIU" stood in silence for "a few minutes" while the school's president hosted a talk with former MLB player Alex Rodriguez on campus, reported WLRN. The students were protesting the "school's voluntary collaboration with immigration enforcement on campus," the outlet reported. 

FIU charged seven of the students who participated with misconduct, and six received written reprimands. The school also ordered the students to record two-minute "video reflections" explaining their understanding of the school's expressive activities policy and how they will "apply" what they "learned moving forward."

The disciplinary action drew the attention of civil liberties organizations, including the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). On June 18, the group sent a letter to FIU urging the school "to drop the conduct charges and revise its expressive activities policy to protect such expression inside university facilities."

The school did not take action. On August 11, the punished students sued the school and members of its administration. In addition to requesting compensatory damages, the suit argued that FIU's Regulation 110(3)—which prohibits "protests, parades, marches, picketing, demonstrations, and other similar expressive activities" inside university buildings—"blatantly violate[d] the Plaintiffs' First Amendment rights" and should be declared unconstitutional. The rule also states that "university indoor facilities are designed for instruction, study, reflection, group discussion, research, administrative functions, and other University activities and operations," and "this provision will be enforced in a content and viewpoint neutral manner."

Becerra, citing the Vietnam War-era free speech case Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, found that the plaintiffs were "substantially likely to prevail" in their challenge against FIU's unconstitutional policy. The ruling also notes that "based on the evidence submitted to date, it does not appear that any Plaintiff, or anyone else wearing an 'ICE OFF FIU' T-shirt, spoke or did anything other than sit, stand, and walk."

According to Inside Higher Ed, university officials have "previously maintained that the policy is compliant with the First Amendment and Florida laws." It's unclear whether FIU will appeal. A school representative told Axios that the university would "comply with the court's order while considering our legal options." 

Regardless of whether one agrees with the students' message, FIU's punishment of the silent protesters should concern free speech defenders. Perhaps the most disturbing part of FIU's punishment was forcing students to record video apologies for silently and non-disruptively expressing their views. Bret Weinstein, a longtime opponent of campus cancel culture, weighed in on the situation, writing on X, "Commitment to freedom of speech requires us to oppose compelled speech every bit as strongly as we oppose censorship." Hopefully, by this school year, other universities will adopt this principled stance.

title: Can Daniels Rewrite Norvell’s Story at Florida State?
description: Can Ashton Daniels rewrite Mike Norvell’s story at Florida State? The Seminoles have plenty to prove, and Daniels could be the key to turning a season of doubt into one nobody saw coming.
fullText:
Florida State is less than 50 hours away from taking the field for thefirst time in 2026, giving the Seminoles their first opportunity to prove thenaysayers wrong and show that this year will be different.

For many around the college football world, having actual football totalk about couldn't come at a better time. Between TROs, injunctions, questionsabout how conferences will handle NFL players returning to college, anduncertainty over how conference rulings will hold up in court, it will be abreath of fresh air to finally focus on the game on the field rather than thechaos surrounding it.

And for Mike Norvell and his Noles, who have faced a consistent wave ofnegativity all offseason, the time has come to write their own story. Resultsaren't determined online or in the papers; they're decided on the field. Whileanalysts have already written a story that ends with change coming toTallahassee, the Noles now have an opportunity to rewrite that ending and provetheir doubters wrong.

"The great thing about it is there can be a lot of narratives out there,but we still get to write the story, and that's been our focus," Norvell said.

Coming off two disappointing seasons and entering the season on one ofthe hottest coaching seats in America, Norvell needs this story to be a fairytale that only Walt Disney himself could have written.

With the over/under win total set between 5.5 and 6.5 wins, depending onthe sportsbook, expectations don't exactly suggest Norvell will have the kindof season needed to write another chapter in Tallahassee.

And many fans wanted Norvell's story to have already ended, let alonehaving this season to continue writing it.

"I think a lot of the fans wanted to move on from Mike Norvell," DannyKanell said. "They're kind of waiting for what feels inevitable that, oh, thisseason's going to be a disaster. They're going to have to move on from MikeNorvell."

If Florida State is going to have a fairytale season and defyexpectations, the Seminoles will need starting quarterback Ashton Daniels tostep up and become the hero of the story.

The former Stanford and Auburn transfer enters the season as the No.13-ranked starting quarterback in the ACC, according to Steven Lassan of AthlonSports.

The good news for Norvell is that Daniels won't have to be Superman. Hecan be Batman instead. He'll need to rely on intelligence, preparation andsmart decision-making rather than trying to make superhuman plays every week,which he had to do at previous stops.

At Stanford, he was surrounded by limited talent. At Auburn, he tookover the starting role late in a season that was already over, with a firedhead coach and players already focused on their next move.

At Florida State, Daniels will need to protect the football, make smartdecisions and be more of a game manager rather than feeling like he has to takeover the game. His 24-22 touchdown-to-turnover ratio doesn't inspireconfidence, but there are reasons to believe he can be that QB they need towin.

The biggest reason for optimism is that Daniels has never had asupporting cast like the one surrounding him at Florida State.

He'll have receivers like Duce Robinson, a potential All-American, alongwith Micahi Danzy and Jayvan Boggs, if Boggs can remain healthy and stay on thefield. He'll also have true freshman Jasen Lopez, who has been competing withBoggs for the starting slot receiver spot.

Daniels will also have a running game he can lean on in  OusmaneKromah and Samuel Singleton Jr. Both can make big plays and grind out the toughyards to extend drives so Daniels doesn't have to.

Norvell put his faith in Daniels early, naming him the startingquarterback out of spring practice. Now, it's time for Daniels to proveNorvell's assessment was right, silence his own naysayers and show he's betterthan many think.

Daniels ' success could ultimately determine whether Norvell's story inTallahassee comes to an end or whether another chapter is written next season.

title: Daniel Lyons Out to Prove He’s The Vocal Leader For Florida State
description: Daniel Lyons enters 2026 with confidence, leadership as he looks to become the anchor of Florida State’s rebuilt defense.
fullText:
With more than 60 new faces on the roster and an entirely different energy surrounding the program, Florida State's defensive turnaround won't hinge on one single player or position group.

For the Seminoles, improvement will require contributions across every position group.

But if there is one returning defender positioned to make a significant leap, it is defensive tackle Daniel Lyons.

Lyons enters the 2026 season with confidence that borders on conviction, yet it is confidence rooted in production and experience rather than empty talk.

"I got a lot to prove still," Lyons said. "A lot to prove to me, people in the building, my coaches, my teammates, and people in my room."

That mindset is noteworthy considering what Lyons already accomplished a season ago. The veteran defensive lineman earned Florida State's Most Improved Defensive Player award after posting career highs with 26 tackles, 3.5 tackles for loss, two sacks and a forced fumble. Across four seasons, Lyons has appeared in 42 games with 13 starts, steadily developing into one of the Seminoles' most dependable interior defenders.

The next step isn't simply becoming a reliable starter. Lyons wants to establish himself among the ACC's best defensive tackles.

"That I'm that. That I'm really like that. I'm that," Lyons said. "Relentless, everything. I'm just that player, I'm just that guy."

The numbers suggest that belief isn't misplaced.

According to Pro Football Focus (PFF), Lyons finished 2025 with a 69.0 overall defensive grade, highlighted by an impressive 73.0 run-defense grade. More importantly, he ranked fourth in the ACC among returning FBS defensive tackles who played at least half of their team's defensive snaps.

That ranking places him behind only Pittsburgh's Francis Brewu, Nick James and Virginia Tech's Kemari Copeland.

Those grades reinforce what Florida State's coaching staff likely already knew. Lyons consistently won against the run while flashing disruptive ability as a pass rusher.

Just as valuable as his production is the leadership role he has embraced.

With a roster undergoing massive turnover, Lyons understands experienced voices need to make themselves heard. He prefers leading through effort, but he has no hesitation speaking up when standards aren't being met.

"Being a leader, I just lead by example," Lyons said. "I work hard. I try to push everybody. If I see somebody slacking, I'll say something to them. Even if they see me slacking, say something to me."

That accountability has become one of the defining characteristics of Florida State's rebuilt locker room.

One theme echoed throughout preseason camp has been the absence of individual agendas.

Lyons believes the Seminoles' willingness to accept criticism from teammates, regardless of age or status, has strengthened the culture.

"It helps us. There's no 'ME' guys," Lyons said. "If I say something to you, it's not that I'm trying to criticize you or down talk you, I'm trying to make you better because we've got to be one."

For a program looking to climb back into ACC contention, that mentality may prove just as important as sacks or tackles for loss.

Florida State doesn't necessarily need Daniel Lyons to become the next Corey Simon or Ron Simmons overnight.

It needs him to become the player he believes he already is the difference maker the team can lean on through thick and thin.

If his leadership continues to elevate the locker room and his production follows the trajectory established in 2025, the Seminoles will have one of the conference's most impactful defensive tackles anchoring the middle of their defense.

fullText:
Former FloridaState Seminoles running back Roydell Williams will continue his professionalfootball journey after signing with the Detroit Lions.

The Lions running backroom has been decimated with injuries, and Williams adds a much-needed body atthe position.

Williams presumablywill back up starter Jahmyr Gibbs, who signed a three-year, $67.5 millionextension with the team, and was added to Detroit's roster after RaheemBlackshear was placed on injured reserve. Williams and Gibbs were teammates atAlabama during the 2022 season.

Aftergoing undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, Williams later signed with the IndianapolisColts as an undrafted free agent. He was waived by the Colts last week, andgained four yards on three carries against the New England Patriots in lastweek's preseason game.

As atransfer from Alabama, Williams played at Florida State during the 2024 and2025 seasons. However, injuries limited Williams to 11 games in the garnet andgold, rushing for 99 yards and two touchdowns during his time in Tallahassee. Williamswas a member of the Crimson Tide's 2020 national championship team.

The 2023season with the Tide was his best season, as he rushed for 560 yards and fivetouchdowns. Against USF that season, Williams rushed for a season-high 129yards and a touchdown in a 17-3 victory.

A top 100 highschool recruit and No. 9 running back nationally by 247 Sports, Williams rushedfor almost 6,000 yards as a prep star at Hueytown High School. Alabama coachNick Saban sent assistant coach Charles Huff to make the recruiting pitch thatwould bring the No. 5 overall prospect in the state to Tuscaloosa.

Thescouting report on Williams showed he was physically gifted for the position,having spent a lot of time in the weight room. The scouting report on Williams showedhe was projected as a power five starter in college and an early to middleround draft pick.

That scoutingreport proved to be inaccurate.

Once atAlabama, Williams shared carries with Jase McClellan in 2023, and was relegatedas a backup on the depth chart behind Gibbs in 2022, Brian Robinson Jr. in2021, and Najee Harris in 2020. That prompted Williams to enter the transferportal in 2024, landing at Florida State.

Williams waspart of a Florida State rushing attack in 2024 that gained only 1,079 yards andscored just eight rushing touchdowns in 12 games. For his part, Williams added53 yards and two touchdowns.

Lastseason, Williams rushed for just 46 yards and no touchdowns, and averaged justa little over three yards per carry for a Seminoles team that was the No. 1 rushingoffense in the ACC.

The NFL finalcut-down deadline has been moved up to Aug. 30 at 6 p.m. ET. With the Lionsfranchise desperate for depth at the running back position, it remains to beseen if Williams survives the cut-down to the 53-man roster mandated by the NFL,or is one of those let go in the roster reduction.

title: Opinion - Tuesday’s election results could spell real trouble for Florida Republicans
description: Did Angie victory "hand Republicans a November Gift”? Quite the opposite.
fullText:
There was a political earthquake in Florida on Tuesday evening that could create prediction-shifting tremors — not only up until the midterm elections, but right through the 2028 presidential election. That earthquake was personified by far-left Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), who absolutely crushed Alex Vindman, the Democratic Party's sanctioned and favored candidate.

The morning after, while I was still trying to wrap my mind around the shocking upset, I came across a piece from RealClearPolitics titled: "Florida Democrats Hand Republicans a November Gift." I believe the message of the headline is way off the mark. For me — and for several Republican operatives I spoke with this week — Nixon's decisive victory represents a neon red warning sign for Florida Republicans.

In recent years, many pundits have claimed Florida to be "deep red" politically. I don't believe that to be the case. I do believe Gov. Ron DeSantis has proven himself to be an exceptional governor, saving the state from the draconian dictates rolled out during the COVID-19 pandemic. But unfortunately for the Republican Party, DeSantis is not on the ballot in November. Neither is his highly capable wife, Casey DeSantis — a woman who, at one point, was considered a lock to succeed her husband, had she chosen to run.

It was not to be, and Tuesday just made it official. The Republican nominee for governor is Rep. Byron Donalds (R), the handpicked candidate of President Trump. And handpicked or not, Donalds may be sailing into some turbulent water.

The first sign is that although Donalds won the primary, a majority of Republicans voted for other candidates. One reason was the devastating ads challenger Jay Collins ran against him — ads that Democrats will ensure have a second life from now until November.

I have spoken with numerous Republicans in Florida, and none wanted Donalds as the nominee. Not one. Is that indicative of how the election will go in November? Maybe not, but these are Republicans who desperately want to keep Florida red.

Next is the victory by state Rep. Angie Nixon (D). Give her some props — Vindman and the entrenched Democratic Party outspent her about 16 to one, and she still humiliated him. But is her victory more about her strengths and connection with voters, or is it part of the growing voter dissatisfaction — and outright anger with incumbents — that we see sprouting up across the country? If it is the latter, which I believe it is, then that also spells trouble for Donalds and the Republican Party of Florida.

Not only is Nixon the new, new thing but Donalds is part of the old, old thing — most especially for young voters, the working class, and non-white voters. Rising star or not, Nixon is going to bring out a bunch of new voters. And even if they may not be able to put her over the top against Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), they will likely vote against Donalds while checking the box for Nixon.

It has been reported that there are 1.5 million more registered Republicans in Florida than Democrats. On paper, that seems to signal a slam-dunk for Donalds. But not so fast. A certain percentage of that 1.5 million identified as Republicans only because of support for DeSantis. Some share will stay home since DeSantis is not on the ballot in November. Some of them are angry with Trump for endorsing Donalds and not giving Casey DeSantis the proper time or respect to evaluate a potential run. Some share aren't very impressed with Donalds, as the primary results demonstrate.

Nixon got more than 700,000 votes during the Democratic primary in deep red Florida.  Only a fool would underestimate her potential in the general. The promise of free stuff has worked since the invention of politics. Pardon the pun, but that promise will partially trump Trump and his various endorsements.

While not running against him, Nixon will still be an X factor in the eventual Donalds vote total — one that doesn't even take into account Democratic primary winner for governor David Jolly, nor how much money the national party will pour into Florida.

So did the Nixon victory "hand Republicans a November Gift"? Quite the opposite. I believe it has energized the Democratic base in the state while opening more eyes to the possibility that Florida is not as nearly as red as some have come to believe.

Donalds was mostly off the voter radar screen as a congressman. But now that he is the Republican nominee for governor, he is going to come under increased scrutiny. The betting odds may still list him as the favorite come November, but no one I know will be shocked if he goes down to defeat.

If I were the Republican leadership, I would cut out the personal attack nonsense and start addressing the issues that most matter to the working class.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

title: 8 South Florida cities among 'worst' real estate markets in state, says new report
description: South Florida cities are among the worst real estate markets in the state, according to a new study by WalletHub.
fullText:
Miami Beach is among the worst real estate markets in the U.S., according to a new study by WalletHub — within the state itself, markets in South Florida populate the lower ranks.

In the Aug. 19 report, the personal finance company evaluated 300 cities of "varying sizes" across "two key dimensions" — real estate market, along with affordability and economic environment. WalletHub "evaluated those dimensions using 17 relevant metrics" in order to "determine the best local real estate markets."

The full list of metrics, which were assigned various weights, can be found at the bottom of the report. They include characteristics such as home value forecast, median days on the market, share of seriously underwater mortgages and ratio of rent price to sale price. Each metric was "graded on a 100-point scale, with a score of 100 representing the healthiest housing market."

Among the 300 cities surveyed, Miami Beach ranked as number 294, with a total score of 39.33. The city had a real-estate market rank of 293 and an affordability and economic environment rank of 228.

In Florida alone, Miami Beach ranks at the bottom, followed by Hollywood, which ranked 285th overall. The latter city received a total score of 43.13, with a real-estate market rank of 283 and an affordability and economic environment rank of 170.

Other South Florida cities among the bottom two hundred included West Palm Beach, which ranked at 241 with a total score of 48.75, Sunrise, which ranked at 244 with a total score of 48.41 and Pompano Beach, which ranked at 271 with a total score of 45.74.

The Miami market itself, however, ranked among the top 40 nationally. At number 38, the city had a total score of 60.28, a real-estate market rank of 30 and an affordability and economic environment rank of 167. It was also the most highly ranked Florida market.

"Current home prices are extremely important, but there's much more that you need to look at when determining the health of a city's real estate market," said Chip Lupo, an analyst for WalletHub. "Factors like the cost of living, the potential for the value of homes to increase, the availability of recently-built homes and the quality of the city's job market are all important to consider in conjunction with asking prices and interest rates."
